title: Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Cleveland Browns recap: Big second quarter, clutch kick fuels win and first place in AFC North
summary: The Steelers put together a touchdown-scoring drive that lasted nearly ten minutes in the first quarter. But then, in the second quarter, it was all Cleveland, as they scored three consecutive touchdowns to go up 21-7. Pittsburgh tried chipping away over the rest of the game, as a few Browns turnovers helped keep them in […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 01: Denzel Ward #21 of the Cleveland Browns celebrates with his teammates after an interception against Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers during the first quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 01, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Steelers put together a touchdown-scoring drive that lasted nearly ten minutes in the first quarter. But then, in the second quarter, it was all Cleveland, as they scored three consecutive touchdowns to go up 21-7. Pittsburgh tried chipping away over the rest of the game, as a few Browns turnovers helped keep them in it. Mid-way through the fourth quarter, a field goal by the Browns extended the team’s lead back to eight points. Then, it was up to the defense to finish the game. The defense did their job at first, but then it was up to the offense to close it out. They were on their way to doing that, but then Watson missed a wide open target that could have sealed the game essentially. Instead, Pittsburgh got the ball back, Rodgers got hot, and had Pittsburgh in the red zone. On a fourth down, a pass interference flag kept them alive, and they got the touchdown and two-point try to tie things up at 24-24. Instead of going to overtime, though, K Andre Szmyt drilled a field goal from 56 yards out to put the Browns up 27-24 with ten seconds to go. Cleveland held on and improved to 3-1 — holding sole possession of first place in the AFC North for the moment. Let’s get to the full game recap. 1st Quarter – Steelers vs. Browns The Browns received the opening kickoff, but a holding penalty made them start further back. Cleveland started with three positive plays, but it ultimately led to a 4th-and-1, and head coach Todd Monken wasn’t willing to gamble early. After P Corey Bojorquez’ quick punt, Pittsburgh began at the 22 yard line. It looked like Pittsburgh might go three-and-out too, but on 3rd-and-11, a quick screen to WR DK Metcalf picked up 15 yards and a first down. A few plays later, on 3rd-and-3, QB Aaron Rodgers got rid of it quick again to Metcalf for 7 yards and another first down. He was flagged for a taunt after the play, though, which pushed Pittsburgh back by 15 yards but kept it a 1st-and-10. Rodgers kept keeping things simple, checking it down to RB Jaylen Warren for an open 11-yard gain into Cleveland territory. A few plays later, after a run by Pittsburgh, DT Mason Graham was down on the ground, with trainers tending to him. He walked off under his own power, but was taken to the blue medical tent, with Pittsburgh having a first down at the Browns’ 38 yard line. Two plays later, DT Maliek Collins collapsed the pocket and nailed Rodgers for a sack, setting up 3rd-and-16. Rodgers checked it down to a receiver, but three penalties were called on the defense, with the one being accepted being a roughing the passer shove called on Collins to give Pittsburgh at first down at the 20 yard line. A few plays later, on 3rd-and-1, a run moved the chains to set up 1st-and-goal at the 9 yard line. Two plays later, a flip to the motion man, WR Roman Wilson , along with blocks on the edge to seal it, resulted in a 12-yard touchdown pass that gave Pittsburgh a 7-0 lead. It was 17-play, 73-yard drive that took up almost 10 minutes of clock. Take it home Rome‼️ @Trilllroman 📲 Stream on NFL+: https://t.co/vqIDzYZB2x pic.twitter.com/tioBXAEJxD — Pittsburgh Steelers (@steelers) October 2, 2026 The Browns began their next drive at the 35 yard line after a touchback, and came out aggressive. QB Deshaun Watson found WR KC Concepcion for a 21 yard gain. KC making it happen for 21 yards! #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/sgFEteirRX — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 Watson then delivered two deep balls to WR Denzel Boston . Both were very well thrown balls, but the rookie couldn’t haul either one in. The second of the two passes also had clear pass interference from the Steelers defender, but the referee did not throw a flag, forcing a punt. Bojorquez got off a beauty that WR Malachi Corley downed at the 1 yard line. Unfortunately, before they could take advantage of the Steelers being pinned back, DE Jared Verse was flagged for encroachment, and a run by Warren followed by a pass to Warren set up a 2nd-and-1 at the 23 yard line to end the quarter. 2nd Quarter – Steelers vs. Browns Two plays into the second quarter, Rodgers made a terrible decision and was picked off on a downfield throw by CB Denzel Ward — although to Ward’s credit, it was a great read by him too. Cleveland took over at their own 44 yard line. that's our ball thank youuuu #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/0DXjoynSKe — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 A short run by RB Quinshon Judkins for 3 yards was followed by a quick out to an open TE Harold Fannin for 13 yards into Pittsburgh territory. A crossing route to Judkins added 12 more yards to the Steelers 28 yard line. On 1st-and-10, who would’ve guessed that RB Jaleel McLaughlin would get the handoff, make a nice move at the perimeter, and go 28 yards for the touchdown to tie the game at 7-7 — Cleveland’s first rushing touchdown of the year. Jaleel movin' and groovin' for the score! #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/b2xqYWjjGJ — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 The defense held Pittsburgh to a three-and-out and a quick punt. On the first play of their third series, Watson found Boston wide open for a big catch-and-run for 60 yards to the Steelers 14 yard line. 60 YARDS DOWN THE FIELD FOR DB! #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/9rrJl5NINH — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 A quick hitter to Concepcion for 5 yards was followed by a slip screen to Judkins for 7 yards, to the 2 yard line. Judkins finished the drive with a 2-yard touchdown run to put the Browns up 14-7. Quinshon muscling it in! #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/1DH9KmMN8D — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 Pittsburgh got a big run for 24 yards from Warren on the next drive. Pittsburgh worked their way into scoring range, but then DE Isaiah McGuire sacked Rodgers on 3rd-and-4, back to the 30 yard line. K Chris Boswell came on for a 47 yard field goal and missed it to the left! A few plays later, a screen pass to Concepcion worked for 25 yards, as he weaved in and out of traffic. Cleveland had favorable timing, getting inside the red zone and then a goal-to-goal situation with under two minutes to go. On 3rd-and-goal from the 2 yard line, DE T.J. Watt jumped offsides, but it didn’t matter, as Watson quickly hit TE Harold Fannin for a 2-yard touchdown to put the Browns up 21-7. I LOVE HAROLD FANNIN #PITvsCLE on @NFLonPrime pic.twitter.com/UH4gsEGues — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) October 2, 2026 Needing a big play, Rodgers found Wilson wide open up the seam, and then he weaved through traffic to the tune of 49 yards. DT Mike Hall also was helped off the field with an injury. The defense still held tough after that, though, holding Boswell to a 31-yard field goal to make it a 21-10 game at the half. Looong gains 💨 @Trilllroman 📲 Stream on NFL+: https://t.co/vqIDzYZB2x pic.twitter.com/i2Qp1ocKpe — Pittsburgh Steelers (@steelers) October 2, 2026 3rd Quarter – Steelers vs. Browns Pittsburgh got the ball to begin the second half. Unlike their lengthy first half drive, this one was quick: a three-and-out with two stuffed runs and an incomplete pass. The punt, though, paired with a hold by the Browns, pinned Cleveland back to the 4 yard line. They got some breathing room with one first down, but then had to punt after that. Pittsburgh then went three-and-out, as DT Adin Huntington sacked Rodgers on third down to force a punt. Cleveland started their next drive at the 16 yard line, but runs of 7 yards by Watson, 9 yards by Judkins, 6 yards by RB Raheim Sanders , and 9 yards by Judkins helped get the ball out toward midfield. title: Steelers expected Joey Porter Jr. to start versus Browns tonight; what happened?
summary: When the Pittsburgh Steelers kick off versus the Cleveland Browns on Thursday Night Football, they will do so without CB Joey Porter Jr. The Steelers star cornerback is now the Dallas Cowboys star cornerback after a late-night trade on Wednesday night. The process that led to the Porter trade started percolating in the offseason, with […]
full_text: When the Pittsburgh Steelers kick off versus the Cleveland Browns on Thursday Night Football, they will do so without CB Joey Porter Jr. The Steelers star cornerback is now the Dallas Cowboys star cornerback after a late-night trade on Wednesday night. The process that led to the Porter trade started percolating in the offseason , with Pittsburgh’s policy of not negotiating extensions during the season creating an artificial, if not solid, deadline for a deal. Porter then missed the first three games of the Steelers’ season but seemed on track for Week 4 on the road versus AFC North rivals, the Browns. Porter was listed as a full participant in walkthroughs on both Monday and Tuesday , with a note that it was “not injury related”, but a more active practice on Wednesday saw Porter ruled out with a back injury . According to Albert Breer, Pittsburgh fully expected Porter to start this week prior to Wednesday’s practice: This was the week they’d agreed to bring him back, with the team set to play on Thursday against the Browns. He was listed as an estimated full-go for practices on Monday and Tuesday (estimated because the team had walkthroughs both days), lined up with the first defense in walkthrough, and the coaches went into midweek expecting him to start in Cleveland. From starter to ruled out to on another team. Wednesday was the straw that broke the camel’s back for the Steelers: Instead, Porter showed up for what was very light work on Wednesday, told the coaches his back was acting up, and pulled himself from practice, delivering the team a surprising blow a little over 24 hours before the game. At that point, the trust between the team and Porter, already strained, was severed. So the Steelers aggressively shopped him, aiming to get him off the roster before kickoff. Pittsburgh acquired a 2028 second-round pick as well as a late pick in 2027, which Breer reported is based on Porter’s playing time this season. The Cowboys valued the pick they sent as a third-rounder, which they likely could receive as a Compensatory Pick if Porter signs a big deal elsewhere in the offseason. Not exactly a huge haul for a starting-level cornerback whom the Steelers expected to start tonight against the Browns. Are you surprised that the Steelers gave in and how quickly the trade happened? title: Dallas Cowboys: Reading Between the Line vs. Houston Texans
summary: Every week, we’re digging into the trenches, because that’s where the real action happens. We shine the spotlight on the Dallas Cowboys offensive line, who’s holding it down, who’s opening holes for the running backs, and who’s keeping Dak Prescott clean. Let’s get to it. Trench Dashboard Here are the Cowboys offensive line metrics for […]
full_text: Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images | Getty Images Every week, we’re digging into the trenches, because that’s where the real action happens. We shine the spotlight on the Dallas Cowboys offensive line, who’s holding it down, who’s opening holes for the running backs, and who’s keeping Dak Prescott clean. Let’s get to it. Trench Dashboard Here are the Cowboys offensive line metrics for the 2026 season so far. Pass Block Win Rate – 50% 16th Run Block Win Rate – 67% 31st Pressure rate allowed – 28% 10th Sacks allowed – 3 (2nd) Last three week trend: Pass pro good, run blocking improving The Pressure Point Every opponent will look at the Cowboys offensive line and ask, where can we break it? Here’s what to watch for. PRESSURE POINT: Terence Steele has a Will Anderson Jr. problem There is no need to overcomplicate the biggest concern for Dallas this week. Will Anderson Jr. is playing outstanding football. Against Indianapolis last week, Anderson produced nine pressures from only 32 pass-rush snaps. PFF credited him with three sacks and gave him a 93.3 pass-rush grade for the game. Official NFL statistics credit Anderson with 2.5 sacks in the game and four through three weeks. Anderson was on the left side of its defensive front, meaning many of his snaps naturally bring him toward Dallas’ right tackle. Steele has already been the more concerning tackle in pass protection this season, while Tyler Guyton has taken a noticeable step forward on the opposite side. Anderson can win in several ways. He is quick enough to race around the outside, but he also has the strength to drive a tackle backwards toward the quarterback. PRESSURE POINT: Houston can squeeze the pocket from both directions Stopping Anderson does not end the problem. Danielle Hunter is on the opposite edge. His start statistically has been quieter with four pressures and one sack, but this is a player who generated 92 pressures across the 2025 season. Houston also has Sheldon Rankins attacking through the middle. Rankins has six pressures and a 72.3 PFF pass-rush grade through three games. If Anderson pushes Steele backwards from one side while Hunter does the same from the other, Prescott normally has room to step forward. If Rankins is also winning through the middle, that escape route disappears. That is how Houston can create sacks without having to blitz heavily. The good news is Dallas has allowed only three sacks through three games, so the protection has generally held up well despite Smith’s absence. Keeping that number low against this front would be one of the offensive line’s best performances of the season. Where to attack Every defensive line has a weakness, here’s the Texans soft spots and where the Cowboys offensive line should attack. GREEN LIGHT: Run toward Danielle Hunter, not Will Anderson Houston does not have an obvious weakness against the run. The Texans have allowed only 260 rushing yards through three games at 3.5 yards per carry, with opponents yet to reach 90 rushing yards in a game. But Dallas still has to run the football, the key is choosing where. Anderson currently owns a 91.0 PFF run-defense grade. Running repeatedly toward him would be asking for trouble, Hunter is a different story. His current 50.6 run-defense grade ranks 88th among qualifying edge defenders. That gives Dallas a target. When Hunter is lined up opposite Tyler Guyton, Dallas should test that side with Javonte Williams. Let Guyton use the strength he has shown as a run blocker and make Hunter repeatedly defend rather than rush Prescott. Guyton’s development is particularly encouraging here. He currently carries a 79.6 PFF run-blocking grade, sixth among offensive tackles. That is strength against weakness. Dallas finally established a running game against Baltimore. It should not abandon it just because Houston has impressive season-long rushing numbers. GREEN LIGHT: Attack Sheldon Rankins in the running game There is another possible opening inside. Rankins has provided useful pass rush production, but his run defense has been significantly weaker. His current 41.5 PFF run-defense grade ranks 100th among qualifying interior defensive linemen. This is where Tyler Booker and Cooper Beebe should become important. Booker has been one of Dallas’ best run blockers this season. Through the available PFF data, his 78.6 run-blocking grade ranked ninth among guards. Dallas can put Booker and Beebe together on combination blocks against Houston’s interior defenders. That is exactly the type of physical football Dallas showed more of against Baltimore. Houston is good against the run overall, so these yards will not necessarily come easily. But Dallas does not need five yards every time. Four yards on first down is useful because it keeps Anderson and Hunter guessing. The Chaos Report Here’s the Houston Texans defensive trends for this season at the defensive line. Sack Total – 11 (3rd) Pass Rush Win Rate – 42% 30th Run Stop Win Rate – 31% 10th QB Pressure Rate – 23% (26th) Last three week trend: Pass rush trending up Matchup of the week Terence Steele vs. Will Anderson Jr. This may be the most important individual offensive-line matchup Dallas has faced this season. Anderson is not simply playing well. He is currently one of the most disruptive defenders in football. Steele struggled at times against Baltimore and was also responsible for a costly holding penalty that removed an important Dallas first down. If Steele handles Anderson himself, Dallas can leave tight ends in the passing game and allow running backs to release into routes. If Steele needs constant help, Houston begins dictating what Dallas can do offensively. That is why this matchup affects much more than two players. Best route to success: Stay out of third-and-long and make Houston’s edge rushers defend the entire playbook rather than simply hunt Prescott. Injury Updates: Nothing to add to the Cowboys, but Tyler Smith can officially return from injured reserve after this week. For Houston, Jadeveon Clowney and Mario Edwards Jr. are both questionable. Kayden McDonald went to IR with an ankle injury two weeks ago.

title: Making sense of the Cowboys non-existent pass rush
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are struggling to get to the quarterback. Three games into the season, the team as a whole has two sacks. One of those came from Caleb Downs strip/tackle of Jaxson Dart in the opener, but even he didn’t get the pleasure of bringing him down because the ball popped into the hands […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys are struggling to get to the quarterback. Three games into the season, the team as a whole has two sacks. One of those came from Caleb Downs strip/tackle of Jaxson Dart in the opener, but even he didn’t get the pleasure of bringing him down because the ball popped into the hands of an offensive lineman who took off running. The only other sack the team had came in the same game, but it was shared between Donovan Ezeiruaku and Jonathan Bullard, who collectively collapsed on Dart. That’s it. Two lousy sacks. And it’s hard to get sacks when they’re not pressuring the quarterback very much. The Cowboys have a pressure rate of14.4%, which ranks 23rd in the league. They are just not creating much of a disruption in the backfield. But why? There is no obvious answer to this question. Many question the quality of talent on the edge, as it features a combination of young draft picks and newly acquired veterans. The guys doing most of the heavy lifting on the edge include: Donovan Ezeiruaku (69%), Rashan Gary (66%), Malachi Lawrence (34%), and Von Miller (24%). Are these guys just not cutting it? Or does this have more to do with the defensive scheme of new defensive coordinator Christian Parker? The answer consists of a little bit of both, and looking over the game film of the first three games we can compile a laundry list of explanations for their ineffective pass rush. Here they are in no particular order. They don’t seem to have a plan. The rushers aren’t utilizing any creative pass-rush strategy. No stunts, twists, or disguised looks to create pressure. It’s just predictable, straight-up rushes. They’re not winning . This defensive scheme relies on the edge players winning their one-on-one matchups on the outside, but it’s not happening. They are being outmuscled, they don’t offer much of a hand battle, and aren’t showcasing any pass-rushing moves to maneuver around their blocker. They are often wild and undisciplined. When they attack, they fly all over the place. They don’t seem to be in sync with any type of collective plan or responsibility. They act as independent soldiers who will sometimes become victimized by their own aggression, allowing quarterbacks an easy escape route. They can never finish. There will be times when the energy is there, and it sure looks like they’re about to get someone, but at the last second, the quarterback gets loose. Too often, they just get caught out of position, where they are left reaching and lunging, only to come up empty. Off-balance tackling attempts won’t cut it. Things get a little chippy. Sometimes the Cowboys’ edge rushers had to navigate through multiple blockers to get to the quarterback. The Ravens approached this very wisely and employed a tight end or running back to chip the rusher at the line of scrimmage. These were very effective, as they disrupted the timing and forced the edge rusher to take a more scenic route to the quarterback, where they never arrived at their destination. They were protecting against the run. One thing about this edge-rushing group is that most of them are antsy to dart inside and snatch that running back for a huge tackle for a loss. This split-second delay in assessing the play impedes their get-off, putting them in a tough spot right out of the gate. They hang back in coverage. These guys are not pin-their-ears-back pass rushers. At. All. They’re multiple, remember? Whether it’s defending the run or sliding back into coverage, they have a variety of responsibilities. Even if they were effective in their pass-rushing reps, this element of their game would always suppress their number of pressures. The Cowboys need to be better at generating a pass rush. Failure to do so is really a strain on their secondary, especially considering how banged up that unit is. They need to find ways to get these guys to be more effective. Another part of this is that they’re never going to be great at this. The way the defense is set up, these players have a lot of responsibilities and none of them are elite pass rushers. They’re versatile players who the team is hoping can provide a good balance of pass rush and run support. Is it going to get better? Probably. The young players are still developing, and they should be more effective as they improve elements of their game. It’s a little more discouraging for the veterans. There’s still a chance that things start to fall into place a little better and they become a solid group that can more effectively carry out their plan, but don’t be surprised if there are more bumps along the way. What do you see as the biggest issue with the pass rush?

title: 2026 Week 4 rooting guide for Cowboys fans
summary: Last week, Dallas Cowboys fans felt the impact that other teams’ games can have. On Monday night, while we were still reeling from Dallas’ big letdown in Brazil, the Eagles crashed and burned against the Bears. It lifted our spirits, kept the NFC East more manageable, and has us looking ahead to Week 4 with […]
full_text: Photo by Wagner Meier/Getty Images | Getty Images Last week, Dallas Cowboys fans felt the impact that other teams’ games can have. On Monday night, while we were still reeling from Dallas’ big letdown in Brazil, the Eagles crashed and burned against the Bears. It lifted our spirits, kept the NFC East more manageable, and has us looking ahead to Week 4 with greater optimism. In addition to a much-needed win for Dallas against the Houston Texans, what else should Cowboys fans be rooting for this week? NFC East teams Rams d. Eagles Cardinals d. Giants Colts d. Commanders This is an easy week to freely root against our divisional rivals. Despite offseason hype, the Rams are just 1-2, making a Philly loss far more important to all of the Cowboys’ goals. And if the Eagles drop two straight, especially with this one at home, can you imagine how that crowd is going to turn on them? The Giants got a gift last week with the Titans, who may be the worst team in the league, and are at 2-1. While they’re far from a great team themselves, the Cardinals will present more of a challenge. How Jameis Winston reacts to New York’s acquisition of J.J. McCarthy will be interesting to see. Washington’s coming off a huge upset over Seattle, but this week’s opponent won’t take them lightly. Indianapolis is also 1-2 but just a game back of Jacksonville in the very winnable AFC South. The key matchup will be how QB Daniel Jones, who already has three interceptions this year, handles the Commanders’ opportunistic defense. NFC vs. NFC Bucs d. Packers Panthers d. Lions Falcons d. Saints In the Battle of the Bays, whose continued despair is better for the Cowboys? Dallas plays both of these teams soon: Tampa next week and the Packers in Week 6. The Bucs are 0-3 and down to backup QB Jalon Daniels. Even if they get a win and some confidence this Sunday, they still face a short week traveling to Dallas for Thursday Night Football . Meanwhile, Green Bay is on the verge of collapse. Matt LaFleur is under fire, Jordan Love is shaky, and there’s renewed mockery of Micah Parsons. If they beat Tampa, weak as they might be, it could stop the bleeding and perhaps help them find momentum again. But a loss? That just might send them into a total spiral, and that would be great for the upcoming game against Dallas and for removing an obstacle from NFC contention. Wanting Carolina over Detroit is a simple choice. The Lions are 2-1 and the Panthers are 1-2, plus Detroit is more likely to hit a stride and become a problem in the NFC. If the Cowboys can get to 2-2 this week, it’d be nice to be looking up at as few other teams as possible. The Falcons and Saints are both 1-2 and neither is particularly threatening, so this kind of a toss-up. New Orleans feels a little closer to figuring some things out and being a tough team, so we’ll root against Kellen Moore’s crew. NFC vs. AFC Jets d. Bears Dolphins d. Vikings Broncos d. 49ers Chargers d. Seahawks The AFC could help Dallas out a lot this week! Minnesota and San Francisco are still undefeated, while Chicago and Seattle are 2-1. If the Cowboys can get their stuff together and go on a run, we’d love for things like home-field advantage and even the number-one seed to still be on the table. Any or all of these NFC contenders getting knocked down a peg would be positive for us. AFC vs. AFC Browns d. Steelers The Cowboys’ future draft picks are getting more entangled with Pittsburgh all the time, with the Joey Porter Jr. trade just the latest development. We still own the Steelers’ 2027 fourth-round pick, so we’ll keep rooting for them to lose and push that pick as early into Saturday afternoon as possible. The rest of the AFC-only matchups have no real impact on Dallas, so root according to your fantasy teams or whatever other personal feelings you have.

title: Winless Texans stand in way of Cowboys righting their season
summary: For the first time since 2024, it is time for the Governor’s Cup to be played in week four between the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans, a NFC vs. AFC battle of Lone Star State pro football teams. This will be the first early kickoff game of the season for the Cowboys, and with it […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 18: Head coach DeMeco Ryans of the Houston Texans celebrates a touchdown scored by Derek Barnett #95 after recovering a fumble against the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter in the game at AT&T Stadium on November 18, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time since 2024, it is time for the Governor’s Cup to be played in week four between the Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans, a NFC vs. AFC battle of Lone Star State pro football teams. This will be the first early kickoff game of the season for the Cowboys, and with it coming on October 4th, this will also be the earliest date on the calendar these two teams have met since their first-ever meeting on September 8th, 2002. Yes, this was the first game in Texans franchise history, and they started with a bang beating the Cowboys at home 19-10. Despite the latest installment of this game coming so early, both Brian Schottenheimer and DeMeco Ryans, and their teams, will feel like they’ve faced more than their share of attrition and adversity in the early going of this 2026 season. The Cowboys are 1-2 through three games for the third year in a row, with a record of 1-0-1 in their last two week four contests in this spot. Amazingly, this is the second year in a row the Texans are 0-3. They stopped their slide last season also in week four with a home win, 26-0 against the Tennessee Titans. This will be the first meeting between these two teams where they both enter with a losing record. It will also be the latest in a season the Cowboys are playing an opponent still searching for their first win since also doing so in week four of 2019 at home against the Miami Dolphins. Having the focus and attention to detail to hand these desperate teams another loss is something the Cowboys have struggled with more recently. Last season’s Bears game comes to mind for the Cowboys in this spot. The Ben Johnson era in Chicago began with two divisional losses to the Vikings and Lions, but they became the Caleb Williams-Ben Johnson Bears against last year’s woeful Cowboys defense, the start of four straight wins for the Bears. The Cowboys will be hoping they already put this type of game behind them from a defensive standpoint, especially in the ‘big plays allowed’ department, in Brazil against the Ravens. They come out of the international game with two safeties, P.J. Locke and Jalen Thompson, injured and set to miss extended time, but draw C.J. Stroud and a Texans offense that’s struggled mightily to push the ball downfield. Stroud is on pace for his lowest completion percentage since coming into the league in 2023, has not thrown an interception yet but been sacked ten times with one of them being a strip sack, and been the signal caller for an offense that’s collectively gone 16 for 44 on third down in three losses. These 44 third downs faced are tied for the second most in the league so far. Houston also went 0-4 in the red zone and scored only six points at home in week two against the Bengals, a very disappointing response after taking the Buffalo Bills to the wire in week one. The Texans’ biggest offseason addition to be more dynamic offensively was not at receiver or tight end, but running back David Montgomery. The right formula has not been there to get Montgomery going, as he’s faced the highest percentage of eight man boxes in the league by nearly 2.5% more than the second place back Ashton Jeanty. The reason the sky is not falling in Houston for a winless team as much as it is further north in Texas for the 1-2 Cowboys is because not only were the Texans in this spot last year, but they became the seventh team since 1981 to make the playoffs after an 0-3 start. Even more amazingly, the Texans were also the most recent team to do this prior to 2025, in 2018 with an 11-5 finish. This is the same record the 1992 San Diego Chargers finished with, despite starting 0-4, and still to this day they are the only example of a team starting 0-4 and making the playoffs. DeMeco Ryans, the head coach that’s taken H-Town to the Divisional Round of the playoffs the last three years, will get to dig in and prepare as the fourth straight defensive-minded head coach to play the Cowboys this year. Ryans will likely find a lot to like about how John Harbaugh and the Giants, and Jesse Minter and the Ravens, took the game to the Cowboys offense in big spots. Throw in the pressure and expectations around Dallas being exponentially higher than they are in Houston, despite pressure on this being a crucial year for Stroud and Ryans to take another step, and it will be the visiting head coach under the most pressure compared to the winless one in Sunday’s game. In a very weird way despite the Cowboys-Texans rivalry only going back to 2002, and the Cowboys only having 10 head coaches in their franchise history going back to 1960, the Texans have been a common opponent in seasons that turned out to be very significant for Dallas head coaches many times before. The 2002 Cowboys that began the year with a loss to the Texans moved on from HC Dave Campo after finishing 5-11, hiring Bill Parcells for 2003. Parcells wouldn’t coach against the Texans until 2006, beating them at home in week six that season, but again this was a head coach’s final year in Big D. Parcells was replaced by Wade Phillips in 2007. In 2010, Phillips would get his first win of the season in week three against the Texans in Houston. Losing his next five games though, Phillips was fired mid-season and replaced by Jason Garrett. Garrett became the first Cowboys head coach to last for multiple matchups against the Texans when he beat them in overtime in 2014 at home, and lost in overtime on the road in 2018. Mike McCarthy would follow this by beating the Texans in 2022, but losing by the biggest margin the Cowboys have ever lost to the Texans by in his final season of 2024. That was a Monday Night Football primetime game in Week 11 of this season, and Cooper Rush versus Stroud at quarterback. KaVontae Turpin provided the lone Cowboys touchdown from 64 yards out in the second quarter, cutting a 14-0 Texans lead in half, but Houston would pull away 34-10 to win it. The current Cowboys aren’t built to be thinking about 2029 in any way, shape, or form, the next time they’ll see the Texans. All they need to focus on is seeing Schottenheimer right the ship and get to 2-2 in his first opportunity against the Texans. Doing so would turn the narrative, even just a little bit, on this run of Schotty calling plays against defensive head coaches, a run that will continue in week five against Todd Bowles and the Buccaneers. The Cowboys and Texans have alternated wins and losses in this series starting with that 2014 meeting, and with the Texans winning the most recent one in Dallas, this pattern continuing would see the Cowboys get their first win in Houston since 2010. History says the Texans are absolutely playing for their postseason lives, and the Cowboys are looking for their first win against a team not in their own division since last Thanksgiving. Tensions are high on both sides and something has to give, with the Cowboys returning from Brazil and Texans coming home from Indianapolis off their first loss to the Colts since 2023, and first at Indy since 2021. The Colts had a balanced approach on offense with Daniel Jones throwing it 36 times, Jonathan Taylor running it 23 teams as part of 31 rushes total, while Josh Downs and Tyler Warren led the Colts in targets. Old-timers Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell made big plays as well, including on the final drive that ended in a go-ahead 53-yard field goal for the Colts. This would be as good of a time as ever for the Cowboys to look at how the Colts, Bengals, and Bills played the Texans and play their own brand of complementary football to calm everything down, even just a little bit.
author: Sean Martin

title: Cowboys team has a great chance to get back on track in Houston
summary: The trip to Brazil ended in one of the most painful ways possible for the Dallas Cowboys. Dallas fought Baltimore all the way to the final second, only for Tyler Loop’s 56-yard field goal to give the Ravens a 34-31 victory. That leaves the Cowboys at 1-2. But there are plenty of reasons to believe […]
full_text: Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images | Getty Images The trip to Brazil ended in one of the most painful ways possible for the Dallas Cowboys. Dallas fought Baltimore all the way to the final second, only for Tyler Loop’s 56-yard field goal to give the Ravens a 34-31 victory. That leaves the Cowboys at 1-2. But there are plenty of reasons to believe Dallas can travel to Houston and come home with its second victory of the season. The first reason is becoming increasingly obvious, Dak Prescott is playing some exceptionally good football. Through three games Prescott has completed 73 of 105 passes for 730 yards, seven touchdowns and only one interception with a passer rating of 107.2. Thanks to Dak and his leadership, Dallas is averaging over 29 points per game, seventh-best in the NFL. Houston is averaging only 18 points, ranking 24th. That is an important difference. Dallas has shown that it can score enough points to survive difficult games, Houston hasn’t. The Texans are 0-3 and have scored only 54 points across those games, Dallas has scored 88. And Houston’s most recent performance gives the Cowboys another reason for confidence. The Texans faced an Indianapolis defense that had been struggling badly through the opening two weeks and managed only 223 total yards. C.J. Stroud threw for only 167 yards and the entire offense rushed for just 70 yards. That tells Dallas something very important. The Cowboys don’t need a perfect game to beat Houston. They need to play clean football, put points on the scoreboard and force the Texans offense to try and keep pace. Then of course there’s CeeDee Lamb. Through three games Lamb already has 20 catches for 309 yards and three touchdowns. That’s an average of 103 receiving yards per game. His last two performances have been even better. Lamb exploded for 153 yards and two touchdowns against Washington before adding another 112 receiving yards against Baltimore. That gives him consecutive 100-yard games. And he isn’t doing it by simply catching short passes. Lamb is averaging 15.5 yards per reception, with five catches already going for at least 20 yards. Houston now has to work out how to stop him. And concentrating completely on Lamb creates another problem. George Pickens finished the Baltimore game with 82 receiving yards. Another major positive from Brazil was Javonte Williams. The Cowboys struggled to establish their running game over the first two weeks. That changed against Baltimore. Williams carried the ball 19 times for 98 yards and a touchdown, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. That was easily his best rushing performance of the season. He was so effective early that Dallas was repeatedly moving Baltimore off the line of scrimmage. Then the Cowboys defense. Stroud has has already been sacked 10 times through three games. And Houston has been dealing with problems up front. Starting guard Ed Ingram missed the last two games with a groin injury. Houston hopes he can return against Dallas, but his availability remains something to watch when the official injury reports begin later this week. Even if Ingram returns, this line has spent three weeks allowing a lot of pressure to reach its quarterback. That gives players such as Quinnen Williams a matchup they can attack. Dallas hasn’t turned its pressure into enough sacks yet. But sometimes the opponent creates the opportunity. This is a chance for the Cowboys pass rush to finally have its breakout performance. As for the ground game, Dallas’ defense has had problems stopping the run this season. Thankfully, Houston hasn’t exactly looked like a team ready to take advantage. The Texans’ leading rusher is David Montgomery, who has only 103 rushing yards through three games and is averaging just 2.8 yards per carry. Houston ran for only 60 yards against Cincinnati. Then it managed just 70 rushing yards at 3.3 yards per attempt against Indianapolis. Across those last two games, that’s only 130 rushing yards combined. That is significant for Dallas. The biggest concern defensively has been opponents controlling games on the ground and keeping Prescott standing on the sideline. Houston has not shown it can consistently do that. One of the more surprising things about Houston’s start has been its inability to finish drives. Against Cincinnati in Week 2, the Texans reached the red zone four times and failed to score a touchdown on any of them. This is another positive for the Cowboys defense. Another situation worth watching is Nico Collins. Collins caught seven passes for 75 yards and a touchdown in Houston’s opener against Buffalo. He hasn’t played since. A hamstring injury kept him out against Cincinnati and Indianapolis, and Houston is hopeful he can return against Dallas. Dallas enters this game on the road, but it is facing a Houston team that is 0-2 in its own stadium and 0-3 overall. And Dallas doesn’t need to travel thousands of miles this week, they just take the short hop to Houston.
author: Mike Poland

title: Cowboys at Texans: 2 players the Cowboys should use more in Week 4
summary: The Dallas Cowboys head into Week 4 facing a crucial matchup against the Houston Texans. If the Cowboys want to avoid their second-straight demoralizing loss, they’ll need to change some things up on Sunday. With that thought in mind, here are two players the Cowboys should use more in Houston. 1) WR Ryan Flournoy Three […]
full_text: (Photo by Wagner Meier/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys head into Week 4 facing a crucial matchup against the Houston Texans. If the Cowboys want to avoid their second-straight demoralizing loss, they’ll need to change some things up on Sunday. With that thought in mind, here are two players the Cowboys should use more in Houston. 1) WR Ryan Flournoy Three games into the 2026 regular season, Ryan Flournoy has been a virtual non-factor. The third-year wideout came into the year with some high expectations after a very productive 2025 campaign, but so far this season he has struggled to make an impact in Dallas’ offense. Flournoy has caught just nine of 18 targets for 67 yards. His big-play ability has been missing in action, as shown by the 26-year-old failing to record a reception of 20+ yards or more and having just one reception totaling 10+ yards. While not getting Flournoy involved hasn’t hurt Dallas’ offense much so far, if they can get the young wideout playing at a high level, it could make their offense truly unstoppable. If they can block up Houston’s front, the Cowboys should have a chance to move the ball in the air this week against a Texans defense that has surprisingly struggled against the pass. Houston ranks 21st in the league in defensive dropback EPA (0.138) and is 24th in NY/A (6.7) and 26th in passing yards allowed (716). Getting Flournoy going could be the missing ingredient to take the Cowboys offense to the next level. Dallas needs to focus on getting the young wideout involved in Houston on Sunday. 2) TE Brevyn Spann-Ford I probably sound like a broken record at this point, but the Cowboys need to give Brevyn Spann-Ford a legitimate number of reps at tight end. Last week, starting tight end Jake Ferguson’s ball-control issues once again reared their ugly head when the 27-year-old fumbled in a key spot. That fumble was Ferguson’s eighth since the start of the 2024 season, tied for the third-most of any player in the league. Ferguson’s touches-per-fumble rate of 18.9 is by far the highest of any player on the list below. The Cowboys have a MAJOR problem going on with Jake Ferguson. He is up to 8 fumbles since 2024. Ferguson is fumbling the ball at an absurd rate. pic.twitter.com/Uwvt0iwUq2 — Marcus Mosher (@Marcus_Mosher) September 28, 2026 Ferguson’s ball control issues would be passable if he were still a YAC specialist like he was back in 2023, but this is just not the case anymore. Over the course of his last 20 games, Ferguson has posted an uninspiring 3.2 YAC/REC rate. Even when Dallas is getting him the ball, unless he is wide open, he’s not been able to turn short catches into bigger plays down the field. Thankfully for the Cowboys, they have a tight end who is capable of doing just that in Brevyn Spann-Ford. The 26-year-old did just that when given a chance on Sunday against Baltimore, recording one of the highlights of the day on an impressive 19-yard catch-and-run. Nobody could tackle Brevyn Spann-Ford 🤠 @BALvsDAL on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/YQlDi8vHWN — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Every week it’s becoming clearer that Spann-Ford might just be the best tight end on Dallas’ roster. This week they need to take that into account and give him just as many opportunities as Ferguson.

title: 2027 Dallas Cowboys draft picks following Joey Porter Jr. trade
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have been busy as of late. We are only at Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season, but they have been wheeling and dealing draft picks related to 2027 for some time now, and Wednesday night was the latest example. The Cowboys struck a deal with the Pittsburgh Steelers to acquire veteran […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have been busy as of late. We are only at Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season, but they have been wheeling and dealing draft picks related to 2027 for some time now, and Wednesday night was the latest example. The Cowboys struck a deal with the Pittsburgh Steelers to acquire veteran cornerback Joey Porter Jr. and they spent a second-round pick in 2028 to do so, along with a sixth-rounder in 2027. The details around Dallas’ 2027 draft allotment are a little fuzzy with all of the deals they are doing, three of which have come with Pittsburgh specifically, so we have organized what they have to work with. 2027 Dallas Cowboys draft picks following the Joey Porter Jr. trade Round 1: The Cowboys own a first-round pick, but it is the worse of theirs and Green Bay’s. Dallas has Green Bay’s by way of the Micah Parsons trade, but they owe the better of the pair to the New York Jets as a result of the Quinnen Williams trade. 2: The Cowboys own their second-round pick. This is the easiest one in the entire discussion. 4: While the Cowboys do own a fourth-round pick, it is not their original one (more on that shortly). They own Pittsburgh’s fourth-rounder as it came to them in the Broderick Jones trade. 7: Similarly, the Cowboys do not own their original seventh-round pick. The one that they have came to them by way of the Nate Thomas trade. That deal happened with the Houston Texans, but Houston held the pick by way of the New England Patriots. What happened to the other picks?! You might be wondering where the rest of the picks went. Round 1: As noted, the better of the two they own will belong to the Jets. This hasn’t technically happened yet, obviously. 3: The Cowboys dealt this to Pittsburgh in the Broderick Jones trade. As they got the fourth back, it was effectively a pick swap. 4: Dallas dealt their original fourth-round pick to the Green Bay Packers to acquire Rashan Gary. 5: The Cowboys sent this pick to the Steelers as well, but it came in last year’s George Pickens trade. 6: The Cowboys just sent this pick to Pittsburgh as a part of the Joey Porter Jr. deal. 7: Dallas’ original seventh-round pick went to the Philadelphia Eagles in the trade down during this past draft’s first round. Philly jumped up to select Makai Lemon and Dallas moved down before selecting Malachi Lawrence. It should also be noted that Pittsburgh sent Dallas their 2027 sixth as a part of everything involved in the George Pickens trade, but the Cowboys sent it back to the Steelers in the Broderick Jones trade. What are the net results between Dallas and Pittsburgh specifically? As you can see, the Cowboys and Steelers have really enjoyed finding one another on the proverbial dance floor as of late. It is important to note that the three trades they executed were all separate, but it is interesting to see the net results between them. Cowboys Received: George Pickens Broderick Jones Joey Porter Jr. 2027 4th Steelers Received: 2026 3rd (from Pickens trade, became Drew Allar) 2027 3rd (from Jones trade) 2027 5th (from Pickens trade) 2027 6th (from Porter Jr. trade) 2028 2nd (from Porter Jr. trade) And again, that 2027 sixth that originally belonged to Pittsburgh also passed hands through Dallas before returning. Oh, and Mike McCarthy used to coach the Cowboys and now coaches the Steelers. Got it? Good.

Though the Panthers are 1-2 and the Lions are 2-1, both teams are very much considered a competitor for their respective divisions, and both are looking for a defining win to silence some of the doubters. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 8: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions hugs Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers after the game at Ford Field on October 8, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. The Lions beat the Panthers 42-24. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers face off on Sunday night in a litmus test game for both franchises. Though the Panthers are 1-2 and the Lions are 2-1, both teams are very much considered a competitor for their respective divisions, and both are looking for a defining win to silence some of the doubters. The Lions are currently 3.5-point favorites according to FanDuel Sportsbook, but this one could be even closer than that. Let’s break down the matchup in this week’s On Paper statistical breakdown, preview, and prediction of Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers Note: We are throwing away all 2025 data. Everything listed below represents 2026 only, unless otherwise stated. Lions pass offense (12th) vs. Panthers pass defense (16th) Through the first three weeks of the season, I expressed a healthy amount of optimism for the Lions’ passing attack given the incredible consistency they’ve shown over the last three years. They’ve rewarded that trust with one of the most efficient passing attacks in football thus far. Through three weeks, the Lions rank: Third in passer rating (116.1) 10th in yards per attempt (7.4) Sixth in dropback EPA (0.286) Fifth in success rate (53.2%) Behind Jared Goff, this remains a top-10 passing attack that’s on the border of a top-five unit. The one thing they have been missing thus far is explosive plays. Through three games, the Lions have just nine passes of 20 yards or more, ranking 14th in the league. In each of the last four seasons, they’ve finished top-five in that statistical category. But teams are playing deep-shells against them and Detroit hasn’t found a way to pierce that coverage. Goff has just three passing attempts with 20 or more air yards (one completion), which is tied with Sam Darnold for the least in the NFL. The good news is that pass protection has been stellar so far for Detroit. Goff has faced a pressure rate of 32.2% (seventh lowest), has a sack rate of 6.0% (15th), while the offense line ranks second in pass-block win rate (60%), but 20th in PFF pass blocking grade. It’s hard to get a firm grasp on the Panthers’ pass defense. In Week 1, the Bears’ offense was just all over them, but they held their next two opponents relatively in check—although neither are the most explosive passing attacks in football. Through three weeks, the stats are inconclusive: Sixth in passer rating allowed (79.0) Sixth in yards per attempt (6.1) 11th in dropback EPA (0.004) 18th in success rate (46.8%) The first two data points are promising, but the last two may fall closer to reality given that the Panthers have faced two mediocre-at-best passing offenses—and have mostly seen the damage done on the ground . The main talking point about the Panthers’ passing defense has been the loss of their two starting cornerbacks this week. Both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn were placed on IR this week, leaving Will Lee and Akayleb Evans to step in. Admittedly, both players have flashed at time and won’t be pushovers, but they still represent significant downgrades. Carolina’s pass rush is better on paper than in practice thus far. Free agent defensive end addition Jaelan Phillips (12 pressures, 2.0 sacks) is an outstanding player, as is veteran defensive tackle Derrick Brown (six pressures), yet the overall stats for Carolina’s pass rush are underwhelming. They’re just 21st in pressure rate (24.2%), 19th in sack rate (6.0%), and 23rd in time to pressure (2.70 sec.). Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. The Panthers tend to lean heavy on zone and deep coverage—again trying to take away the explosives. So I expect St. Brown to eat over the middle, especially against less-experienced cornerbacks. Advantage: Lions +1.5. The only way I see the Lions losing this matchup is if the Panthers’ pass rush lives up to its billing finally. Carolina does like to send the extra heat, but Detroit proved they could handle it last week with Goff playing nearly perfect football against the blitz. I’m not sure how the Panthers’ reserve secondary will hold up against the Lions receivers, but it certainly seems like a favorable matchup. Lions run offense (2nd) vs. Panthers run defense (23rd) With the sample sizes so small, I am trying to pull back my optimism of the Lions’ rushing attack, but the early signs are very promising. I want to completely throw out Week 2, because of the injuries the Lions were dealing with on the offensive line, but that’s not completely fair. Still, even with that stinker of a game—in which the Lions also had to abandon the run—the Lions rushing efficiency metrics are optimistic. They rank: Ninth in yards per carry (4.4) 15th in rush EPA (-0.082) Fifth in rush success rate (48.1%) The only reason for Detroit’s low ranking in EPA is the lack of truly explosive plays. While the Lions have 11 rushes of 10+ yards (t-sixth most), they only have a single run over 20 yards to help skew the data this year. But the offensive line stats are stellar in the run game. Detroit ranks fifth in PFF run blocking grade (70.6), fifth in adjusted line yards, and fourth in rushing yards before contact per rush (2.06). This week, you’ve likely heard how bad the Panthers’ run defense is, and to an extent, that is true. However, it’s likely better than you think it is. Their season ranks are: 32nd in yards per carry allowed (5.7) 18th in rush EPA (-0.090) Ninth in success rate (35.6%) Those last two data points required some extra research, and I discovered the following. For one, the Panthers have been disproportionately impacted by quarterback runs through three games. Of their 580 rushing yards allowed, 25% of that yardage was damage done by mobile quarterbacks. That won’t be an issue this week . They’ve also given up a ton of big rushing plays—allowing five (most) rushes of 20+ yards. In between those splash plays, the Panthers have actually been okay. Not good, but okay. But one thing they haven’t done well is create negative plays: Carolina sports the second-lowest “stuffed rate” (rushes of 0 yards or less) in football with 8.9%. Player to watch: Devin Lloyd. Expected to be back after missing a game, Lloyd is the quarterback of the Panthers’ defense. Entering his fifth year and first with the Panthers, Lloyd brings a reputation of being a great all-around linebacker but specifically a stout run defender. He ranked 11th in PFF run defense grade in 2025 (85.2) and ninth in 2024 (84.2). Advantage: Lions +1.5. This could—and should—be the week the Lions break out a long run. And while I expect the Panthers run defense to be stouter than the numbers suggest, Detroit also has one of the best rushing attacks in football right now, and I don’t think the Panthers are equipped to stop them for four quarters. Panthers pass offense (15th) vs. Lions pass defense (26th) Okay, now the bad news. Bryce Young appears to be taking Year 4 by the horns, and is off to a very strong start. Thus far, the Panthers passing attack ranks: 16th in passer rating (95.6%) Eighth in yards per attempt (7.7) 14th in dropback EPA (0.130) 23rd in success rate (44.2%) Okay, so it’s not the most efficient passing attack in football despite ranking first in passing yards per game. The fact of the matter is this is a passing offense that is probably below average on a play-to-play basis, but is capable of an explosive play at any moment. This is highlighted by the fact that Carolina ranks just 28th in completion percentage (59.0), but has produced more 20+ yard passing plays (13) than anyone through three games. Pass protection has been a pretty big issue, with the Panthers allowing a league-high 43.6% pressure rate and seeing that pressure arrive at 2.52 seconds (fifth fastest). They rank 25th in pass block win…

title: Lions vs. Panthers preview: 3 key matchups
summary: It’s “Sunday Night Football” and the Detroit Lions have an opportunity to string together back-to-back wins when go on the road to take on the Carolina Panthers. Readers here at Pride of Detroit are spoiled. Truly. Before even getting to this key matchups article, coverage throughout the week have previewed this upcoming game from many […]
full_text: It’s “Sunday Night Football” and the Detroit Lions have an opportunity to string together back-to-back wins when go on the road to take on the Carolina Panthers. Readers here at Pride of Detroit are spoiled. Truly. Before even getting to this key matchups article, coverage throughout the week have previewed this upcoming game from many different perspectives. From Meko Scott and Morgan Cannon’s “Before the Roar” podcast, Erik Schlitt’s scheme breakdown , Ryan Matthews’ 5 Q’s , and much more from the rest of the staff and even beyond with Pride of Detroit Direct . All of that to say, as I begin finding my own space here I hope to provide thoughts and insights with these weekly key matchup previews that meet that standard set and go beyond the surface level. Digging deeper into not only what the matchups mean for each individual player, but for the team as a whole. Not only what the matchups may dictate for each particular game, but with future in mind as well. Every week I could write about which team is going to run the ball well and which is going to stop the run. I could write about the one-on-one wide receiver and cornerback matchup du jour every week. Rinse and repeat. I’d rather not. And I’d bet you’d rather something more than that as well. Time to dig in. Ennis Rakestraw Jr. vs. Ennis Rakestraw Jr. Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. showed flashes in his first action on the season against the Jets. His performance is by far the most meaningful development of any individual player through three games. If you’re reading this, I do not need to give you the numbers to prove the struggle of the Lions cornerbacks not only this season, but throughout the entirety of Dan Campbell’s tenure. I do not need to remind you about the multiple starters that necessitated a release due to off-field incidents. I do not need to remind you about the potential trade acquisition of Joey Porter Jr. that Brad Holmes did not make. What I may need to remind you about is that while Rakestraw is in this third year, he is just 24 years old. He was highly-touted, and often mocked to the Lions as a first-round pick in 2024 pre-draft coverage. He finished as the 32nd-best player on Daniel Jeremiah’s final big board. “About Ennis Rakestraw, has never been about his kind of what he could do and his skill set and what we were seeing on the field,” explained Kelvin Sheppard. “It had nothing to do with any of that. It was always about his availability with Ennis.” I could make this a matchup between Rakestraw and wide receivers Tetairoa McMillan or Jalen Coker, but I do not believe either player is Rakestraw’s biggest obstacle for successful in primetime. “I learned that I can play in this league,” Rakestraw said after his 2026 debut last week . “I finally got to play in a game, and I knew what kind of challenge it was going to be backside with No. 5, he’s paid a lot of money. Just had to step up to it.” If Rakestraw can continue his upward trajectory into Sunday night and begin to establish himself as a starting cornerback, the perception of and outlook for the defense will shift dramatically. But it’s up to him. Ennis vs. Ennis. “Just like I told [Ennis] Tuesday when he was in here. I said, ‘How much you play is up to you,’” Sheppard said. “We saw a very small sample size. Now lets see what that looks like on a larger scale and we’ll just take it from there.” Lions pass rush vs. Bryce Young The next key matchup of the contest I wanted to specifically highlight the pass rush as it relates to quarterback Bryce Young, not the Panther’s offensive line. There are a few reasons for this. First, the Panther’s offensive line is banged up with starting tackle Ikem Ekwonu on reserve/PUP, guard Damien Lewis not practicing with an elbow, and rookie first-round pick Monroe Freeling limited in practice in concussion protocol. With that being the case, I fully expect the Lions pass rush to have an advantage against the offensive line. At the bare minimum, Aidan Hutchinson and Alim McNeill should be to win their individual matchups relatively consistently. Per NFL Pro, Bryce Young currently faces the second-highest pressure rate among qualifying quarterbacks at 43.5% with the fifth-quickest average time to pressure of 2.56 seconds. On the other side of the equation, the Lions’ defensive pass rush is in the top-10 in pressure rate at 39% with the second-quickest average time to pressure of 2.46 seconds. The question is not whether the pass rush will create pressure quickly, but whether Young handles the pressure well and whether his ability to extend plays will result in explosive results. While under pressure, Young’s completion percentage sits at 49%, boosted by a 5.01% completion percentage over expected. Interestingly, under pressure his air yards per attempt is 14.3 while just 7.8 when not pressured. This feels like a make-or-break opportunity for the Lions, who are in the top five in explosive passing plays allowed this season. But with this tenancy evidenced in the metrics, there is an opportunity for Sheppard and Lions defenders to be cognizant of and to appropriately scheme against Young’s disparate pattern of throwing the ball further down field when feeling the heat. Jameson Williams vs. Ejiro Evero If you ran to the Panthers roster see if Ejiro Evero was one of the backup cornerbacks being thrust into a starting role due to the injuries of both starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson put them on IR , you probably aren’t alone. Ejiro Evero is one of the better defensive coordinators in the NFL, leading the Panthers defense since the 2023 season. The key matchup here is about how Evero decides to scheme against the Lions’ most feared offensive weapon. Not Jahmyr Gibbs. Not Amon-Ra St. Brown. Over the first three weeks of the season, the box score would tell you that Jameson Williams has been relatively absent from the Lions offense compared to expectations. But a deeper analysis shows just how much Williams has an effective on the game and how he implants fear deep within the soul of opposing defensive coordinators. “I was talking to [Jared Goff] about Wednesday out on the practice field,” said Sheppard. “Because Saint and Jamo were like, ’why are all of these defenses going to these 2-high? Scary. They’re scary.‘ I said, ‘Yeah, I’d be scared of ya’ll two as well.’ But the big thing its a consensus around the league if you look at it, most touchdown drives, there is an explosive pass play on the drive. It’s a real thing, guys.” The Panther’s run a significant amount of zone coverage defensively (85.2%), with the vast majority of that being cover-3 zone at 48.7%. Defensive coverage rates through Week 3 Via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/m6XO0Z3Cbs — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) September 29, 2026 The question is going to be how the Panthers intend to handle Williams’ speed as he stretches the deep center of the field vertically, stressing free safety Nick Scott. Expect offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to test this matchup early to get as much information as possible as to the Panthers defense. Critically, defenses have remained committed to their deep shell-coverage against Williams. But eventually the dam will break. Enough Gibbs and St. Brown gut punches play-by-play and drive-over-drive while still resulting in a consistently cool 31 points of offensive production will force someone to flip the switch. When that game comes, watch out. Will it be you, Ejiro Evero? Three key matchups. Three opportunities.

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Panthers in Week 4
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-1) and Carolina Panthers (1-2) will close out the Sunday slate of NFL games in Week 4, when the two battle it out on “Sunday Night Football.” “Going out to their place, ‘Sunday Night Football,’ Charlotte, North Carolina,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of this upcoming matchup. “It’ll be loud. It’s going […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 08: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions points at the line of scrimmage against the Carolina Panthers at Ford Field on October 08, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (2-1) and Carolina Panthers (1-2) will close out the Sunday slate of NFL games in Week 4, when the two battle it out on “Sunday Night Football.” “Going out to their place, ‘Sunday Night Football,’ Charlotte, North Carolina,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of this upcoming matchup. “It’ll be loud. It’s going to be one of those environments that we’ve got to be able to have poise under those circumstances. They’re coming off of a loss, and so they’re going to want to make that right. At home, big game for them. So, we’ll get their best shot […] This will be a good test. We’re looking forward to it.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Panthers in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1800 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 3.5-point favorites in Week 4 . Panthers base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 4 preview: Breaking down the Panthers’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Jared Goff beats Panthers blitz, thrives by taking what’s given Lions quarterback Jared Goff has been sensational through the first three weeks of the season, sporting the third-highest passer rating in the NFL at 116.1 and producing a 0.22 EPA per dropback, seventh-best. He’s been efficient against zone coverage (0.17 EPA, 13th), man coverage (0.54 EPS, 8th), in the red zone (0.55 EPA, 8th), and against the blitz (0.29 EPA, 8th). The Panthers run a bend-don’t-break version of Vic Fangio’s defensive scheme (see our weekly scheme breakdown for more details ). Their typical approach to defense is to cede short yardage plays to prevent explosives, force offenses to drive the length of the field on double-digit drives, and bank on offenses making a critical mistake before they reach the end zone. Despite the passive approach, the Panthers have surprisingly altered their approach this season by increasing their blitz rate: 44.4% overall (4th highest) and 37.6% on passing plays (7th highest), per NFL Pro. So, why would a defensive scheme known for its willingness to cede yards in small increments blitz so much? As Jeremy Reisman pointed out in his observations from the Panthers-Browns game , the Panthers simply aren’t generating enough pressure with just four rushers: No blitz: 33.3% pressure rate (10th), 2.93 seconds to pressure (22nd) Blitzing: 55.6% pressure rate (fourth highest), 2.76 seconds to pressure (29th) While the Panthers have seen production in this new approach, they may not have the same success against the Lions and Jared Goff. This season, Goff is completing 75.8% of his passing attempts against the blitz (5th best in the NFL) for 8.0 yards per attempt (10th) and four touchdowns. Last week he was flawless against the blitz; the Jets blitzed the Lions on 44% of plays, and Goff responded by completing all 14 of his passing attempts for 148 yards and a touchdown. If Goff can keep beating the blitz, the Lions’ skill players will have huge opportunities to eat after the catch (note: the Panthers have given up 286 YAC through three games, sixth most in the NFL). If the Panthers move away from the blitz and the Lions offensive line can keep him clean against just four rushers, look for Goff to adjust again and simply take what the defense gives him. Goff’s accuracy and risk-averse passes—along with the Lions skill players’ ability to create YAC—should allow Detroit to sustain drives and put up points. Prediction 2: Jahmyr Gibbs breaks 100 yards rushing… again With the Panthers looking to take away explosives, expect the Lions to try and take advantage of base and light boxes by feeding Jahmyr Gibbs. The Lions have leaned on Gibbs through three games (he’s accounted for 51% of the Lions’ offensive touches this season, per NFL Pro), and he’s delivered, producing a 57.8% success rate, the highest in the NFL. On paper, the Panthers’ run defense looks atrocious. They’re allowing 193.3 rush yards per game (last in the NFL), 5.7 rush yards per game (last), 13 rushes of 10 or more yards (29th), a minimal 8.9% stuffed rate (31st), and 3.85 yards after contact (32nd), landing them at 23rd in DVOA run defense rankings. Now, some of those numbers are skewed by a disastrous Week 1, but they still haven’t kept a team under 123 rush yards. Let’s look at how they did in each of their first three weeks: Week 1 vs. Bears (DVOA rushing: 9): 291 rush yards allowed, 7.5 yards per carry Week 2 vs. Falcons (DVOA rushing: 6): 123 allowed, 4.6 YPC Week 3 vs. Browns (DVOA rushing: 31): 132 allowed, 4.4 YPC While the Panthers certainly settled down since their game with the Bears, the Lions have an equally explosive offense and currently hold the No. 2 DVOA rushing attack, averaging 120 yards per game (9th), 4.4 yards per carry (9th), 11 rushes over 10 yards (7th), a rushing success rate of 48.2% (6th), per NFL Pro. In addition to Gibbs’ explosive ability, the Lions’ offensive line has also been getting consistent push in the run game. Despite not having Blake Miller and Christian Mahogany in Week 2, the Lions still average 2.06 yards before contact in the run game, the fourth-best mark in the NFL. Prediction 3: Lions take away Panthers’ rushing attack The Lions will always prioritize stopping the run, but like the Panthers, their numbers look worse than what the defense can actually do because one game skews a small sample size. Let’s take a look at how they did through the first three weeks of the season: Week 1 vs. Saints (DVOA rushing: 18): 91 rush yards allowed, 3.6 yards per carry, -0.03 EPA per rush Week 2 vs. Bills (DVOA rushing: 1): 203 allowed, 5.6 YPC, +0.37 EPA per rush Week 3 vs. Jets (DVOA rushing: 20): 58 allowed, 3.1 YPC, -0.23 EPA per rush Essentially, the Lions did their job against the bottom half of the league in rushing offenses, but struggled mightily against the Bills’ No. 1 DVOA rushing attack. While it’s still early in the season, the Panthers’ rushing attack certainly looks closer to being in the same bucket as the Saints and Jets than the Bills, and the statistics back that up: Panthers (DVOA rushing: 21st): 97 yards per game, 4.3 yards per carry, -0.11 EPA per rush With the defensive changes the Lions implemented against the Jets, several encouraging signs suggest the run defense is trending up. When defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard was asked what he thought his defense did well against the Jets, he pointed to their run defense. “Guys doing their job in the run game, just owning (their) gap. It starts with the front, being physical, changing the line of scrimmage. We want to play on their side of the line, […] We fire off, we get downhill on the second level, and we try to make things happen on their side of the line on our terms. And I think our guys have done that. “They’ve done it pretty well in two out of three games, and we all know what transpired at the Buffalo game. I want to give props to some of those players that had errors in the Buffalo game and the run game. The emphasis they took and the onus they took on to go out and make sure they weren’t a repeat offender.” Prediction 4: Lions disrupt Bryce Young with 4-man pressure Through the first two weeks of the season, we saw the Lions defense utilize the blitz to create pressure. Against the Saints, the Lions blitzed nearly 35% of snaps, then bumped that up to 55% against the Bills. The problem was that the Lions generated a pressure rate of only 43.4%, just slightly above the league average (43%), and were gashed in the secondary after sacrificing a player in coverage. After the Lions’ Week 3…

title: 9 Detroit Lions trade targets after missing out on Joey Porter Jr.
summary: If you somehow didn’t hear the news already, the Pittsburgh Steelers have traded former second-round draft pick Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys in exchange for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. And while I am not among the fans hitting the panic button, more than five weeks prior to the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes arrives at Northwest Stadium before the win against the Washington Commanders in Landover, Md. on Sunday, Nov. 9, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If you somehow didn’t hear the news already, the Pittsburgh Steelers have traded former second-round draft pick Joey Porter Jr. to the Dallas Cowboys in exchange for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. And while I am not among the fans hitting the panic button, more than five weeks prior to the NFL’s 2026 trade deadline , I certainly wouldn’t have minded adding a player like Porter Jr. With that said, in-season trades are difficult to pull off for a myriad of reasons. To start, you have to find a team that is willing to part with a player that, in most cases, can help them in the present—meaning the selling team is not concerned about its roster taking a temporary stepback after trading away a productive player. This requires a front office to have some pretty warm and fuzzy feelings in regards to their overall job security. Rarely is a coach or general manager going to be happy about making their roster worse when they are trying to save their jobs. Adding draft picks to use in the next couple of NFL drafts? Fun! Adding draft picks for your replacement to use when you are looking for another job? Not as much fun! Secondly, the financial aspect of the deal has to make sense for both sides. For instance, let’s say there is a young, established player that just signed a lucrative extension in the offseason. In this example, if the team starts off performing below expectations, they may elect to focus on future assets rather than their current roster. While they may now be looking beyond 2026, trading this example player likely would harm the organization from a salary cap standpoint. Especially so if they have a lot of guarantees tied to the contract, resulting in potentially a chunk of dead salary cap that the team has to eat in the following league year. You get the picture: some players are just not for sale. There are a lot of variables at play to make an in-season trade work. And while it is still too early to definitively say which teams will be looking to sell and which ones won’t, myself and my good friend Anthony Balaj have put together a list for Lions fans to keep their eyes on until the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Furthermore, we have decided to include both cornerbacks and safeties as defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard’s scheme relies heavily on sound safety play. Depth at both positions are arguably thin when considering 2026 and beyond. Cornerbacks Greg Newsome II (26), New York Giants. Currently on a one-year contract : Like the Panthers, the Giants are really banged up at the moment. And since coach John Harbaugh is in his first year at the helm for New York, we could see them being sellers at the deadline if they continue to drop games. Newsome is a former first-round pick by the Cleveland Browns in the 2021 NFL Draft. Listed at 6-foot and 192 pounds, Newsome has prototype size at the position. Garrett Williams (25), Arizona Cardinals. Currently in the final year of his rookie contract : Originally a third-round selection by the Cardinals in 2023, Williams could be someone the Cardinals look to recoup some draft pick compensation from if the new regime is not looking to retain him after the 2026 season ends. Williams returned in Week 3 from an Achilles injury suffered in 2025. Donte Jackson (31), Los Angeles Chargers. Currently in final year of contract : Veteran player with eight years of experience in the NFL and in the final year of what was a two-year deal signed with the Chargers. Most likely would be a rental situation unless the Lions decided to bring him back on a shorter deal with some guarantees in 2027. Mike Hughes (29), Atlanta Falcons. In year two of a three-year contract : If this name sounds familiar, it’s because Hughes appeared in 16 games for Detroit back in 2022. Hughes has been a productive player since entering the league back in 2018, and while he is technically signed through the 2027 season, there is an out for the team given the fact that there is no remaining guaranteed money on his contract after 2026, resulting in only a $1.666M dead cap hit if he were cut. Julius “JuJu” Brents (26), Miami Dolphins. Currently in final year of a two-year contract : Brents is a former second-round pick by the Indianapolis Colts. At 6-foot-3, 198-pounds, Brents has physical traits that present a lot of upside. While primarily an outside corner at this stage of his career, he has some experience at safety in college with signs of urgency in the run support. Deonte Banks (25), New York Giants. Currently in year four of his rookie contract : Another member of the Giants’ secondary that could end up elsewhere by the time the trade deadline arrives. At 6-foot-2 and 200-pounds, Banks possesses ideal traits for the position, but has yet to put it altogether as a professional. New York opted to not pick up his fifth-year rookie option, meaning the former first-round pick would be an unrestricted free agent in 2027. Safeties Andrew Wingard (30), Arizona Cardinals. Currently on a one-year contract: Wingard is a veteran safety with plenty of time on task since being an undrafted free agent back in 2019. Not a game-changer by any means, but with as thin as the Lions’ safety room looks at the moment, he certainly couldn’t hurt things as a value option, especially until star defensive back Brian Branch returns from the Achilles injury he suffered late last season. Jesse Bates II (29), Atlanta Falcons. Currently in the final year of four-year contract : Bates has been one of the better all-around safeties in the game for a while now. And while he will be 30 years old by the time the 2027 season is underway, he could be a player the Lions could bring back on a short-term deal with a good amount of guarantees. He would help in the immediate, and give the Lions a player they could pair with Branch for the next couple of years while they figure out the position’s long-term future. Amani Hooker (28), Tennessee Titans. Currently in year one of three-year extension : Hooker signed a second extension with the Titans in 2025 that has him on the books through the 2028 season. One year younger than Bates, Hooker’s deal is palatable with a $13M cap hit in 2027, and a $16M number in 2028. A former Iowa Hawkeye, Hooker is free safety in the peak of his career. This is the type of player we would not mind giving up a Day 2 selection considering both his performance and future salary commitment, especially given the uncertainty surrounding Kerby Joseph’s status in 2026 and beyond.
