title: Thursday Night Football expert picks, predictions: Steelers at Browns
summary: We’ve already reached the quarter(ish) mark of the 2026 NFL regular season with Week 4 upon us. As Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell likes to point out annually, this is the time of year when we start to really figure out what the identity of each team is after a month full of data. The […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 28: Myles Garrett #95 of the Cleveland Browns pressures Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers during the second quarter at Huntington Bank Field on December 28, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images We’ve already reached the quarter(ish) mark of the 2026 NFL regular season with Week 4 upon us. As Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell likes to point out annually, this is the time of year when we start to really figure out what the identity of each team is after a month full of data. The week kicks off Thursday night with an AFC North bout between the 2-1 Cleveland Browns and 2-1 Pittsburgh Steelers. I think it’s fair to wonder if either of these teams can be seriously considered a contender. The Steelers probably have the better resumé with wins over the Atlanta Falcons and Cincinnati Bengals, but sandwiched between those wins is a 20-3 loss to a New England Patriots team that has looked terrible in its other two games. The Browns, on the other hand, notched narrow wins over the Buccaneers and Panthers, but started off the season by getting boatraced by the Jacksonville Jaguars, 34-10. It’s never easy to win on a shortened week, but both teams have an opportunity to show that their early success is for real, and their one slip-up was just that—a slip-up. Here’s who our staff is picking for Thursday night’s game between the Steelers and Browns. If you don’t see them below, click here for our Week 4 Thursday night picks between the Steelers and Browns . And if you want to watch the game, here’s the game-day information you need: Date: Thursday, Oct 1, 2026 When: 8:15 p.m. ET Where: Huntington Bank Field — Cleveland, OH TV: Prime Video Streaming: Prime Video, Twitch

title: Lions, Panthers injury report: DJ Wonnum returns to practice on Thursday

The Lions got some good news Thursday as starting EDGE DJ Wonnum returned to practice, a great sign for Detroit’s pass rush. Let’s take a look at Thursday’s injury […]

title: Before the Roar: Previewing Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers
summary: We are back with your Week 4 episode of, “Before the Roar,” where myself and my good friend Meko Scott break down the Detroit Lions’ upcoming matchup against the Carolina Panthers. After a close win in Week 3 over the New York Jets at home, Detroit is back on the road in a primetime slot […]
full_text: We are back with your Week 4 episode of, “Before the Roar,” where myself and my good friend Meko Scott break down the Detroit Lions’ upcoming matchup against the Carolina Panthers . After a close win in Week 3 over the New York Jets at home, Detroit is back on the road in a primetime slot where they will be looking to pick up their third win of the season. Coming off of a year where they won the NFC South and took the Los Angeles Rams to the wire in the playoffs, the Panthers have high hopes for the 2026 season, despite getting off to a bit of a rocky start thus far. Going into his third year as coach, Dave Canales has plenty of talent to work with on either side of the ball. Unfortunately, the Panthers are among the most injured teams in the NFL through the early portion of the season. Still, as we know, this is the NFL and, injured or not, no team is to be taken lightly in this league. We kick things off by examining the makeup of the Carolina coaching staff, and what both sides of the ball have looked like through three weeks of play. Obviously, we won’t know who is suiting up or not for the Panthers until later in the week, but either way, there is enough talent on other areas of their roster that make this an interesting matchup for Detroit—especially on the road, and potentially in the rain. Knock on wood for me there. From there we highlight several matchups featuring various position groups, as well as give our predictions for the Sunday night matchup. You can listen wherever you get your podcasts, and you can watch over on the Pride of Detroit Youtube page right here. As always, please be sure to like and subscribe to the POD YouTube Channel. Your support allows us to reach other Lions fans around the world.

title: 6 Detroit Lions coordinator takeaways: Why the increase in zone coverage
summary: It was another news-heavy day from Allen Park, with all three coordinators meeting with the media prior to the Detroit Lions’ Week 4 game against the Carolina Panthers. Here are my biggest takeaways from those press conferences. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Derrick Brown is a problem Panthers defensive tackle Derrick Brown is unquestionably the most […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard of the Detroit Lions during a game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was another news-heavy day from Allen Park, with all three coordinators meeting with the media prior to the Detroit Lions’ Week 4 game against the Carolina Panthers. Here are my biggest takeaways from those press conferences. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Derrick Brown is a problem Panthers defensive tackle Derrick Brown is unquestionably the most talented player on Carolina’s defense. Last year, he produced 5.0 sacks, 11 QB hits, and 39 pressures. Petzing faced the Panthers twice in the last two years, one game without Brown, one with him in the lineup. The difference was staggering. “He’s a force. I think back, I believe when we played them in ’24, he was not out there. And then we played him again in ’25, and it was like night and day because of one guy,” Petzing said. “I mean, he’s a great player, plays hard, plays physical, takes up a lot of space in the run game. Still is dynamic as a pass rusher, which is not always the case for some of the bigger players inside. So, it’s a force that we’ve got to be ready to handle. ” Juice Scruggs is growing Petzing wouldn’t speculate on what the Lions will do with Scruggs when starting center Cade Mays returns from injury around the bye week, but he did talk glowingly of Scruggs’ growth at center. “He works his tail off to make sure he’s on top of it because the communication upfront is going to start with him. In terms of making sure that everything is on the same page, we’re snapping the ball, we’re going in the right direction, we’re in the right play. He’s done a really nice job of that,” Petzing said. “And I think the other piece that we talked about probably is when I first got here was the violence and the attitude that he plays with. He’s a physical player. He plays fast, he plays free.” When it comes to his communication, the early emphasis was on getting Scruggs to communicate loudly and confidently. When asked how that was going, Petzing made a great reference to the movie Anchorman. “I think it comes with confidence of knowing what you’re doing and why you’re doing it. So, it’s not the Ron Burgundy question mark at the end, ” Petzing said. “It’s more like, ‘No, I am Ron Burgundy, and this is what we’re doing. Like, let’s go.’ And I think you’ve seen that kind of develop here over his time in the position now and in the role.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Improvements in the Jets game good, but not enough Sheppard typically begins his weekly press conferences with a recap of the previous game, and Thursday was no different. He was quick to point out some areas of improvement, notably the strides made in the run game (58 rushing yards, 3.1 YPC), and the decrease in explosive plays allowed (seven, after allowing 11.5 per game in Weeks 1-2). But the goal can no longer be just to improve from the week before. Seven explosive plays allowed is still too many. “I stood in front of the room, and I told them, there’s no moral victories in this thing. And what I mean by that, we won the game, but on our side of the ball, let’s not start to measure this off of what we did last week and what we did,” Sheppard said. “No, we have a certain standard for the way we want to play here, a certain output that we want to put out there defensively each week. So, let’s try to get more closer to that bar this week versus chasing what we did in the first two weeks.” Why the increase in zone defense The Lions were one of the heaviest man-coverage defenses in 2025, but that has shifted dramatically through three weeks into the 2026 season. After averaging man coverage on 36% of snaps last year , that number has plummeted to just 19.4% per Fantasy Points . Sheppard gave a thorough answer on why they made the change, pointing to three things: fitting the scheme to the personnel, limited explosive plays, and creating more turnovers. Here’s him speaking on each: Fitting personnel: “What’s best for us? I know what I might want to do, but what’s best for us? And then how does that blend with the way we want to play, the style of defense that we want to put on tape?” Limiting explosives: “That’s kind of a philosophical thing about what’s important to you and what’s important to us coming out of self-scout is trying to dim down some of these explosive plays primarily in the past game. So, we feel like having more of a shell feel to our defense will kind of talk the quarterbacks into more underneath passing games where we can rally and hit versus the ball just chunking 40 yards down the field.” Forcing turnovers : “ It’s hard to have kind of interceptions, plays on the football and man cover with your back turned, kind of in phase, running, chasing all the time versus seeing it. Being able to break and drive on throws and things like that. So, absolutely it has a lot to do with trying to bring the ball back as a defense.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp On kickoff loophole This year, the NFL quietly changed a rule that a holder can come onto the field to hold the kickoff at any time, rather than just when the ball falls off the tee twice. A couple of teams have already exploited that rule by bringing a holder out there (without a tee) , angling the football in an advantageous way to affect the trajectory of the kickoff. Fipp acknowledged it can give the kicker an advantage. “Yeah, it definitely helps. I think some guys more than others,” Fipp said. “It’s something that we played around with a little bit, but yeah.” The league has talked about closing this loophole, but it remains legal to do so right now, and Fipp teased that Detroit may consider taking advantage. “Never know.” Jake Bates’ power an advantage in weather games? Sunday night’s game against the Panthers is forecasted to have some weather elements, mainly a good chance of rain. Fipp said they’ll practice in the elements this week, but he also agreed with a reporter’s assessment that Bates’ low-but-powerful trajectory on his kicks could be an extra advantage this week. “Anytime you drive the ball a little bit, it’s much more conducive to kicking in wind and weather and all that kind of stuff,” Fipp said. “So that really helps him, doesn’t hurt him. But yeah, so that helps. So, there’s different strengths and weaknesses, pluses, minuses for everything you do.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Kelvin Sheppard defends Detroit Lions’ odd hail mary defense
summary: At the end of the first half of the Detroit Lions’ Week 3 game against the New York Jets, the Jets had eight seconds left to cut into Detroit’s lead. On the first play, the Lions deployed a common defense, which was to have several defensive backs lined up deep, and another set of players […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 27: New York offensive players and Detroit defensive players leap into the air to catch a Hail Mary pass thrown by New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith (not pictured) as time expires in the second quarter during a regular season NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions on September 27, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images At the end of the first half of the Detroit Lions’ Week 3 game against the New York Jets, the Jets had eight seconds left to cut into Detroit’s lead. On the first play, the Lions deployed a common defense, which was to have several defensive backs lined up deep, and another set of players guarding the sideline. Given that the Jets had no timeouts left, the Lions were trying to ensure that any play toward the boundaries would be stopped in bounds, forcing the clock to run out, or defend against a hail mary. That defense worked, and Jets quarterback Geno Smith couldn’t find an open receiver by the sideline. That left three seconds left in the half, and the Lions essentially deployed a very similar defense. That raised questions about the strategy, since it doesn’t seem necessary to defend the sidelines anymore, given that a normal play would almost certainly exhaust all three remaining seconds. And by having defenders on the sideline—not in the end zone or not as part of the one-man pass rush—it looks like wasted defenders. I have yet to get a satisfactory answer as to what the point in these players were for Detroit's Hail Mary defense with only 2 seconds left. (Also, why are the Lions CBs playing 5-10 yards off instead of… 30 yards off?) pic.twitter.com/En5ZR4jYXp — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) September 29, 2026 The Jets’ hail mary attempt fell harmlessly incomplete, but it still felt like an unnecessary risk. On Thursday, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard defended the call, citing a specific situation they were defending against—without revealing what it was. “We practice hail marys against that defense every week for six years. There’s a couple different ways you play the hail mary. We essentially have two to three different ways we can combat hail marys. The other alternative—my friend that was on the other sideline [Aaron Glenn]—knows it in and out, because we did it here for four years, and he was ready for it. A couple years ago, there was a certain team who exposed that certain defense, and if they would’ve thrown it to a certain player, we all would’ve been sick to our stomach. Luckily, they didn’t. I won’t reveal to the public what I’m talking about, but those that know, know. So I went into that game not only playing the Jets, but playing Aaron Glenn. […] We’ve practiced for six years that exact sideline defense, it converts against the hail mary and we practiced it every week, and I like where we were at.” It’s not a very specific answer from Sheppard, and it matches coach Dan Campbell similarly vague defense of the play, as well. “You can do one or the other,” Campbell said about not pass rushing on the hail mary. “And I think for us, let’s stay in it. We went back and forth talking about that last one. If anything, you could go last play and let’s just all defend the goal line. We’re not rushing anyway. I mean time, they’re just going to get back there and then let’s be where we’re supposed to be. We know we’re going up for the ball, cover man, get in front of them. I think it’s a little bit of flavor with where you’re at.” Regarding the “wasted” players on the sideline, Sheppard refuted that characterization of those players, noting that by the time the hail mary was thrown, those players were near the goal line. “At the end of the play, you see where they ended up,” Sheppard said. Upon review, he is right that they were by the ball during the play. It’s possible that those players are in place to defend the second wave of Jets receivers around the 5-yard line in case of a deflection back toward the field of play, but Sheppard didn’t provide any clarity. In the end, the Lions are confident they chose the right defense, so don’t be surprised if they play similar situations the exact same way moving forward.

title: Detroit Lions announce low-cost, same-day ticket program
summary: On Thursday, the Detroit Lions announced the beginning of a new ticketing option for fans. In short, the Lions are setting aside a pool of standing-room only tickets available only to purchase on-site on the same day of upcoming Lions home games. Here are the full details, as provided by an official statement from the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 23: Detroit Lions fans celebrate during the NFL 2025 game between New York Giants and Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 23, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday, the Detroit Lions announced the beginning of a new ticketing option for fans. In short, the Lions are setting aside a pool of standing-room only tickets available only to purchase on-site on the same day of upcoming Lions home games. Here are the full details, as provided by an official statement from the team (I have highlighted the key notes): Four hours prior to the announced kickoff time , Gate D East checkpoint opens and guests (must be physically present and subject to availability) will receive numbered wristbands, these wristbands indicate the ability to purchase the $60 standing room only tickets . Once all wristbands have been distributed, those guests can be screened and enter through Gate D. Ticket purchases will be processed and scanned immediately after purchase. Once sold out, all other guests will be notified, and the limited standing room ticket program will conclude. As of now, the Lions will be offering a minimum of 100 of these tickets per game, with a limit of four per person. The tickets are non-transferrable. This program kicks off for Detroit’s next home game this season: their Week 7 contest against the Green Bay Packers on October 25. In the future, the Lions hope to expand this program beyond just standing-room only tickets to include actual seats to the game. Here’s what new Lions president and CEO Rich Haddad has to say about the program. “This program is for our fans and our community. It’s another way we can recognize the energy and support we receive all year long. We are excited to expand access to our games and give more fans the opportunity to experience Ford Field and contribute to the best home field advantage in the NFL.” While it’s only a limited amount of tickets, it’s a neat option for die-hard fans to get into Ford Field during an era in which Lions tickets are becoming less and less affordable and tougher and tougher to acquire.

title: Packers Injury Report: New offensive lineman added to list
summary: The Green Bay Packers were already dealing with Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (quadricep) injuries this week, but rookie offensive lineman Jager Burton (groin) was added to the Packers’ injury list on Thursday. In total, Green Bay has 15 offensive linemen between their 53-man roster and practice squad, so they’re not short on bodies, […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers were already dealing with Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (quadricep) injuries this week, but rookie offensive lineman Jager Burton (groin) was added to the Packers’ injury list on Thursday. In total, Green Bay has 15 offensive linemen between their 53-man roster and practice squad , so they’re not short on bodies, but this most recent injury to Burton can help explain why Travis Glover was getting some looks at right guard on Thursday , as the team could potentially be down three interior offensive linemen who previously made starts for the team in 2026. Banks and Monk, along with defensive linemen Warren Brinson (calf/groin) and Anthony Campbell (ankle), did not participate on Thursday. Burton was a limited participant, as were defensive lineman Karl Brooks (illness), linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (shoulder/concussion) and edge defender Lukas Van Ness (shoulder). Brooks’ status is trending in a positive direction, as he was a non-participant on Wednesday, while Burton (full participant on Wednesday) and Brinson (limited participant on Wednesday) are trending negatively. If Banks, Brinson, Campbell and Monk all miss Sunday’s game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, four of the Packers’ mandatory five scratches for Week 4 will be made easy. The roster is both “oversigned” on the offensive line and defensive line, so the team won’t need to call up a practice squad player for numbers. The last scratch will likely be another offensive lineman, as it’s uncommon for the team to carry more than eight players on a 48-man gameday roster — and the Packers have 11 offensive linemen currently on their 53-man active roster. Players who remain non-participants due to injury for the Buccaneers on Thursday are rookie first-round pick Rueben Bain Jr. (groin/shoulder), tight end Ko Kieft (elbow) and starting quarterback Baker Mayfield (thumb). title: The Packers are giving themselves options at right guard
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ offensive line is in a period of transition, as it appears that both Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler — who were both brought in this week — have a chance at starting against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 4. According to reports from practice, Tomlinson has already been getting the […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers’ offensive line is in a period of transition, as it appears that both Laken Tomlinson and Kevin Zeitler — who were both brought in this week — have a chance at starting against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 4. According to reports from practice, Tomlinson has already been getting the full share of left guard reps in the media-open portion of practices this week, while the right guard position is a little more open-ended. #Packers first OL early in practice: Jordan Morgan-Laken Tomlinson-Sean Rhyan-Donovan Jennings-Anthony Belton. With Kevin Zeitler working off to the right side. Travis Grover was later pulled over from 2nd OL to take some RG reps with Jennings next to Zeitler on side. pic.twitter.com/Ve7rWEwFGV — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) October 1, 2026 On both Wednesday and Thursday, Donovan Jennings got the “start” at right guard, but Zeitler continues to work on the side of the first-team offensive line, where he’s taking simulated reps as a right guard — both in terms of assignment and stance. You can see an example of that in the tweet above, via Ryan Wood of the Green Bay Press-Gazette . It’s an interesting way to go about ramping up Zeitler, who head coach Matt LaFleur has said will take over the right guard position whenever he’s caught up on the offense. On top of that, Travis Glover, who has yet to play on offense in the regular season, also got looks at right guard today. This pushed Jennings out to “the side” with Zeitler, allowing the team to rep three “right guards” at the same time. So who will start at right guard? If he’s ready to execute the game plan, it’ll be Zeitler — per LaFleur’s comments. If Zeitler still needs a little more time to ramp up, it will likely be one of Jennings or Glover. There’s no certain answer right now, just because of the situation the team is in right now. Maybe we’ll get more clarity by the end of the week, but the truth of the matter is that the Packers are giving themselves options and are repping several players in preparation for what should be an Anxiety Bowl between 1-2 Green Bay and 0-3 Tampa Bay, two teams that desperately need a win in Week 4.

title: Time to find out what Packers have in Kaleb Johnson
summary: I’m fully with my colleague Rcon14 when he says the Packers need to go back to square one on offense, particularly on the ground. It seems abundantly clear what they’ve tried to this point — both from a tactical and personnel perspective — just isn’t working and probably can’t work. Mixing in a few new […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Kaleb Johnson #26 of the Green Bay Packers stands on the sideline during the national anthem prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m fully with my colleague Rcon14 when he says the Packers need to go back to square one on offense , particularly on the ground. It seems abundantly clear what they’ve tried to this point — both from a tactical and personnel perspective — just isn’t working and probably can’t work. Mixing in a few new faces on the offensive line won’t make it any easier to run a complex run scheme, so they really have no choice but to get back to basics and try to maul their way to a ground game. And maybe I’m setting myself up as a future recipient of the “Fell For It Again” award, but I think it can work. Maybe it’s the prodigious quantities of copium I’ve ingested, but I really do think they can grind out enough on the ground with revamped offensive line to keep things competitive, and if they can just get to league average pass protection, the passing game should take off. None of those things are a given, though, and the ground game part of that equation hinges on finding a back who can hammer away behind an offensive line doing whatever they possibly can to get vertical displacement. And looking at the Packers’ roster, the player who best fits that profile is (relatively) recently acquired Kaleb Johnson. General manager Brian Gutekunst specifically praised Johnson’s fit for an outside zone scheme when the Packers traded for him, but I think he’s got the wrong read there ( wouldn’t be the first time ), and the intervening three weeks have done nothing to change my mind. Johnson is a 224-pound back who ran the 40-yard dash in 4.57 seconds. To say nothing of what he’s done trying to run outside (short version: it’s bad), Johnson is physically tailor made to hammer away between the tackles. If the Packers are serious about trying to power their way to ground game success, Johnson’s broad shoulders are going to have to carry the load. Can he do it? He’s shouldered a significant burden on the ground before. In 35 college games, Johnson carried the ball 20 or more times on eight separate occasions. Six of those eight came in his final college season, including a whopping 35 carries in his second-to-last college game. It’s true, only about 20% of those carries came in a gap scheme (per Pro Football Focus), which is a far cry from the sort of profile we saw from Josh Jacobs the last two years (42% and 47% of his carries in gap plays in 2025 and 2024, respectively), but I’m willing to chalk some of that difference up to the gulf between the college and pro games. More to the point, the Packers have nobody else. MarShawn Lloyd’s entire running style can be boiled down to the phrase “going nowhere fast,” and Chris Brooks has been counted upon as more of a pass blocker than ballcarrier during his time in Green Bay. If the Packers are going to lean on someone in the ground game, Johnson looks like the default pick. The Packers have been ramping Johnson up, too. He carried eight times in their Week 2 win over the Jets (a career high) and was on the field for 24 snaps during last Thursday’s debacle against the Falcons (also a career high, and the second-most of any Packers back that night behind Brooks’ 27). The Packers certainly seem like they want a look at him, and he should be a good fit for what they’re trying to accomplish. He’ll have some tough sledding this week. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers only surrender 3.1 yards per attempt on the second ground, the second-best figure in the league, and they’ve played against much better rushing attempts than the Packers can offer. (I don’t even have to look that up; anybody they’ve played against is better than the Packers.) Things may open up after that, though. Chicago’s 5.1 yards allowed per attempt is the second-worst in the league, and the Dallas Cowboys rank 29th at 5.0. If the Packers can survive this week, their offensive line may be up to speed enough to do something against some weaker opponents as we head into the middle portion of October. Whatever the Packers are doing, though, Johnson looks like the best fit to be the point man in a new-look ground attack. Can he do the job? It’s hard to say, but it’d be hard to be much worse at this point.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Packers’ offense must go back to square one
summary: The Green Bay Packers have spent the last couple of years, the seasons with Josh Jacobs on the roster, utilizing a fundamentally different running game than they had in Matt LaFleur’s first few seasons in Green Bay. LaFleur had come from the long-storied Shanahan tree of coaches, and had coached with both father Mike and […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Jacob Monk #62 of the Green Bay Packers kneels on the field after a play against the Atlanta Falcons during the fourth quarter of the game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have spent the last couple of years, the seasons with Josh Jacobs on the roster, utilizing a fundamentally different running game than they had in Matt LaFleur’s first few seasons in Green Bay. LaFleur had come from the long-storied Shanahan tree of coaches, and had coached with both father Mike and son Kyle. He was an offensive assistant under Gary Kubiak, a Mike Shanahan disciple, and was Sean McVay’s non-playcalling offensive coordinator in Los Angeles, both of whom had worked together under Mike Shanahan. What all of these coaches have in common, in the times that LaFleur was there, is that they were extremely heavy users of zone blocking in the run game, particularly outside zone. When LaFleur came to Green Bay, the Packers had been utilizing a very similar running game to what LaFleur had come from for over a decade, with Mike McCarthy overwhelmingly preferring the same zone blocking schemes in the run game. The Packers personnel was a great fit for it, as the front office had spent a decade drafting quicker undersized offensive linemen for McCarthy while Aaron Jones was basically lab-built for the system’s requirements at running back. And this mostly worked well for a few years. The Packers offensive line deteriorated, primarily because of David Bakhtiari’s horror-show knee issues, but after the 2023 season, the Packers made an active choice to change their structure. We actually saw it started to take shape in 2023, as the Packers started to reduce their usage of outside zone in favor of pin-and-pull tosses, counter, and the like. These plays still ask for athleticism from their linemen but use an entirely different structure to open alleys for ball carriers rather than relying on horizontal displacement creating creases. An offseason choice before the 2023 season, signing free agent Josh Jacobs and moving on from the aging Aaron Jones, forced the change in system. Jacobs lacks Jones’ natural gliding speed to make the timing of outside zone work, but excelled in the phone booth spaces you have to live in running inside zone, duo, power, and most of the “gap scheme” family. The problem was that the Packers had an outside zone offensive line for a duo running back, and they have spent the past two seasons trying to resolve that issue, with … rather poor results. The signing of Aaron Banks, the drafting of Anthony Belton, and the moving of Sean Rhyan to center all were attempts to get bigger and stronger to be able to move bodies vertically in the running game. And the Packers’ quarterback had changed in this time as well, and he was different than his predecessor in important ways for how this all marries together. Jordan Love is very good, but he’s also very different from Aaron Rodgers. Rodgers spent his entire Packers career operating out of a heavy outside zone running game. When you pair that with play-action, you typically end up with one of two play structures. The most famous for Packers fans would be those deep half-boots, where Rodgers would sometimes end up ten yards behind his offensive line to uncork a deep ball to, most commonly, Jordy Nelson. But the most common is the stereotypical bootleg action, which effectively works as a rollout, and is often accompanied by concepts that look relatively similar to flood, usually with some sort of slide or flat option as the quick check if the edge doesn’t buy the run-action. Running these types of actions regularly requires a pretty agile quarterback and a pretty quick arm action, both things Rodgers had in spades. Love on the other hand, has a bit of a longer delivery, a necessity given his longer arms, but he is also not as agile as Rodgers was. He has the silly body, after all. Now, Love still can run these actions, and has. It’s just not what Green Bay has gone to as much during his time under center. The play-action builds off of gap scheme are more befitting to Love’s game. The run-action is more vertical, giving Love a more traditional dropback structure, and also allowing him to target the entirety of the field rather than cutting it down by two-thirds. This has been particularly important for him when targeting digs, crossers, and short posts, where he has thrived. These actions ask less of Love’s agility, but more of his ability to layer throws with velocity, something he excels at. The reason I bring the play-action up is that the Packers have been stuck between two offenses all season, because the offensive line, the running backs, and the quarterback don’t line up. The offensive line is apocalyptic and has been undersized. Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton, and Jacob Monk are all, ideally, centers. Jennings apparently can’t snap, and Sean Rhyan is playing center so he’s blocking both Burton and Monk there (if Monk is an NFL player at all). The interior group has been legitimately expansion Houston Texans-level bad, but the Packers have at least taken significant steps to fix that problem in the past week, adding veterans Laken Tomlinson, Mekhi Becton, and, most importantly, former Wisconsin Badger Kevin Zietler. What is noteworthy about these three, particularly Tomlinson and Becton, but even Zeitler at his advanced age, is that they do not fit what Green Bay was trying to run during pre-season, which was a lot of outside zone. These players are here to get vertical displacement in the running game. In the coming weeks, expect to see plenty of duo, plenty of inside zone, plenty of power, etc. And with that, you can build a play-action game that mimics the run looks and a play-action game that plays into the strengths of the quarterback. Now, there are two massive open questions remaining. Most importantly, are these guys going to be good enough to get the Packers offensive line out of terrible to just below average? They’ll still be starting Anthony Belton, someone who should have been playing guard from the moment he was drafted, at right tackle. Zeitler, who was good last year, had off-season quad surgery, hence why he did not sign until the end of September. Becton alternates between good and terrible depending on the year. And Tomlinson was solidly below-average last year in Houston after a few mediocre years in New York. The last season of his that you could classify as good was the same year Aaron Rodgers won his final MVP. Even getting this line to just normal bad from the expansion-level atrocity they are right now will be a massive upgrade, and the veteran know-how of this group should hopefully improve upon the mess of missed assignments and bad technique in both the run and pass game the line has shown in the first three games. The second massive question is the running backs. Marshawn Lloyd has been the worst back in the NFL. I’m not talking in EPA or success rate (he’s second-worst in EPA-per-rush and 13th-worst in success rate), I’m talking about having eyes that can see things happening on my screen. Lloyd is dead last in the NFL in rushing yards over expected, and it’s no secret as to why. He’s, by NFL running back standards, blind. before every snap Marshawn Lloyd picks the hole via RNG https://t.co/d0pLWgMsM6 — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 This concern is not new, as it was very prevalent at USC. He was terrible on zone runs, which ask more of his vision, and he was good on gap scheme runs, which largely pre-determine which hole to hit. Even with the scheme change, the Packers should consider finding a different player to take his roster spot, whether that is waiting for the seemingly inevitable Josh Jacobs return at some point, or cutting bait now and finding someone off a practice squad who can at least give you replacement level running…

title: Packers film room: Lukas Van Ness is off to a strong start in 2026
summary: For three seasons the case against Green Bay Packers pass rusher Lukas Van Ness was simple: the tools were there but the production wasn’t. This season has been different so far. Against the New York Jets in Week 2, the production arrived, and the film shows specific reasons for it rather than luck. Van Ness […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Lukas van Ness #90 of the Green Bay Packers sacks Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons during the first quarter of the game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images For three seasons the case against Green Bay Packers pass rusher Lukas Van Ness was simple: the tools were there but the production wasn’t. This season has been different so far. Against the New York Jets in Week 2, the production arrived, and the film shows specific reasons for it rather than luck. Van Ness recorded nine tackles, four tackles for loss, 1.5 sacks, and four QB hits in a 20-17 overtime win. For scale, in nine games last season he had 1.5 sacks and three tackles for loss. The production came, and the tape shows specific reasons why it came. But even more important is where he is showing up that the stat sheet doesn’t necessarily reflect. So far he has recorded 12 tackles, six assists, four tackles for loss, 3 sacks, and four QB hits, while registering 10 total pressures (3 sacks, 4 hits, 3 hurries). Per Pro Football Focus, he has a 20.7% pass rush win rate in true pass sets. Let’s look at how he’s doing it. Setting the edge in the run game First, Van Ness’ ability in the run game this season is outstanding. Against the Jets, he said the defense expected all week that New York would run the ball in the rain and try to win at the line of scrimmage. Van Ness was prepared. The result was that Breece Hall and Braelon Allen combined for 36 yards on 21 carries. He won his run game reps in several different ways. In the first quarterm he pushed tight end Jelani Woods aside to help tackle Hall for a 3-yard loss on first-and-10. In the third quarter he threw right tackle Armand Membou to the ground and then helped bring Hall down for another loss of 3 on second-and-6. Beating a tight end is expected. Putting a first-round tackle on the ground is the kind of play that makes offensive coordinators rethink their run game. His game against Minnesota perhaps foreshadowed what would see this season. Here, Van Ness completely tosses tight end Josh Oliver aside on the Vikings’ outside toss play. The offense on this play is trying to pin the edges inside but Van Ness quickly read the play and the block, and forced the running back to bounce back inside where Van Ness chased him down for the stop. In the Falcons game, he had a couple more stops and solid run defense grade despite the defense overall being below average against the Atlanta run game. He’s perhaps their most reliable edge setter at this point. 4th quarter sequence in week 2 It’s only been three games with the Packers sitting at 1-2, but in that win he was one of the primary reasons why they closed the game out late. The late stand shows Van Ness doing three different jobs on consecutive downs. With 2:40 left in a tie game in the fourth quarter and the Jets facing second-and-10 from their own 41, he dropped into coverage and tackled Garrett Wilson two yards short of the first down. On third-and-2 he stopped Hall a yard short. On fourth-and-1 he beat tight end Jeremy Ruckert inside off the edge and stuffed Allen. After the game, Van Ness gave some insight into how that play went down. He said the call was a pressure from the right side, which let him pinch inside, and he saw the back step up as he came through the backfield. He described his assignment as to “get in that C gap between the tackle and the tight end” against a down block. The pressure call allowed the defense to get bigger bodies inside to jam up the run with Van Ness getting into the C-gap and the linebackers getting to the edges as the force defenders. The stop was a well-designed call by Jonathan Gannon that Van Ness executed at full speed, not just one player improvising. It should also be mentioned that Jonathan Ford also helped blow up the play but received no statistical credit. Pass rush productivity We can’t talk about Van Ness’ pass rush performance without first acknowledging a pretty big shortcoming that he has worked to improve on, which may be the most important driver of change for him in the long term. Offsides penalties have always been a problem for him. Reports out of Packers camp stated that he jumped too often in practice, which carried over into week one against Minnesota. After the game he said the team has stressed ignoring the quarterback’s cadence, and he is now timing his rush off the left tackle’s movement. Reacting to the blocker’s first movement instead of the snap count gives up a little quickness in exchange for eliminating offsides. But in three games so far, he has had no visible loss of explosiveness in the technique tweak. If that holds, it fixes one of his biggest problems. Here in week three, Van Ness gets Jake Matthews turned parallel to the sideline with a jab step inside before swatting away his contact and sliding around the edge. He displays unmatched power on his rush and while he doesn’t have a lot of pass rush moves, what he does utilize can be very effective. He executes a chop and rip move here that is equal parts raw power and perimeter speed. His chop of the blocker’s arm neutralizes the blocker’s ability to lock him up with their outside hand. To get around the edge, he rips under the outside arm of the blocker and takes him for a ride. The pressure on Geno Smith forces him to get rid of the ball quickly, forcing the offense to take a 3-yard loss. His best rushes had a clear structure. He bull-rushed left tackle Olu Fashanu back into Smith, then changed direction and took out Smith’s legs when the quarterback stepped up. Resetting when the quarterback climbs the pocket is something power rushers often fail to do, and it turns a pressure into a sack. He also won without power. In overtime on second-and-16 he beat Membou with a swim move to help sack Smith for a 9-yard loss. That overtime sack mattered: it left the Jets facing third-and-30, and the punt set up Trey Smack’s winning field goal. Outlook The level of play from Van Ness is notable because with Micah Parsons out, he had no star teammate drawing double teams away from him. These were true wins he generated on a line where he is perhaps the best pass rusher available and that’s the best the Packers could have asked for. It didn’t pan out in week three but that was less about Van Ness than it was just a total team letdown. Whether the opposing game plan is run-heavy or not, it suits his game just fine if this is how he’ll produce going forward if remains healthy. The next test is whether his pass-rush wins hold up against offenses that throw more. We’ll get to see more of Van Ness one-on-one with opposing blockers when Parsons comes back too. But the coaching staff and fans have to be encouraged by his fast start.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Here comes Kevin Zeitler to save the day
summary: It just made too much sense. The Green Bay Packers desperately needed help on the offensive line — particularly at guard. There, out on the open market, was veteran Kevin Zeitler, finally healthy after rehabbing a quad injury during the offseason. Packers fans had spent the last few weeks theorizing about the Wisconsin native and […]
full_text: COLUMBUS, OH - OCTOBER 10: Offensive lineman Kevin Zeitler #70 of the Wisconsin Badgers blocks against the Ohio State Buckeyes at Ohio Stadium on October 10, 2009 in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Jamie Sabau/Getty Images) | Getty Images It just made too much sense. The Green Bay Packers desperately needed help on the offensive line — particularly at guard. There, out on the open market, was veteran Kevin Zeitler, finally healthy after rehabbing a quad injury during the offseason. Packers fans had spent the last few weeks theorizing about the Wisconsin native and former Badger All-American coming in to save the day, at least at one position on the line; thankfully, the Packers recognized the fit and made it happen. Is Zeitler really a panacea for everything plaguing the Packers’ offense? Certainly not. But if he can stabilize one of those interior spots and just not let free rushers through on damn near every play , that will go a long way to helping Jordan Love lead a competent offense. Meanwhile, you can put to bed any projection of an outside zone running scheme with the recent changes up front. With the line likely to eventually consist of Aaron Banks or Laken Tomlinson at left guard, Zeitler at right guard, and Anthony Belton at tackle, the Packers will almost assuredly be back on board with the power run game. Hopefully that sets up well for a big back like Kaleb Johnson, even if he played in a zone scheme in college. Zeitler alone won’t save the Packers’ season. The other players and the coaching staff need to do their part. But it does feel like Zeitler’s arrival could be a catalyst that dramatically changes the trajectory of this team’s 2026 campaign. For Packers and Kevin Zeitler, Here’s Why It’s Dream Fit | SI.com It’s not hard to explain: Zeitler is from Waukesha, just outside of Milwaukee. He played at Wisconsin. Now he has a chance to wind down his career in his home state. New Packers OL Kevin Zeitler already making case to start in Week 4 | Packers Wire It’s hard to imagine even a rusty Zeitler playing worse than Jacob Monk has in his three games so far this year. Meanwhile, Zeitler explains when the Packers contacted him: Veteran linemen expected to ‘settle things down’ for Packers up front | Packers.com Between Zeitler and Laken Tomlinson, who took #1 reps at left guard on Wednesday, the team could have a new-look interior line as early as this Sunday. Green Bay Packers offensive line must give Jordan Love time to be himself | Packersnews.com That line has to do enough to let Love cook, because the Packers still can’t rely on the run game right now. But if they can at least keep Love from getting pressured quickly all the time, he’s plenty good enough to lead a solid offense. title: NFL predictions: Houston Texans run it back against the Dallas Cowboys
summary: How are we here again? Your Houston Texans are 0-3. The offense, full of weapons, is struggling to put more than 18 points per game on the board and suddenly, this is a must-win match up against the Oklahoma South Cowboys. Fanduel ‘s odds currently have the Texans down by 3. Will Kaimi Fairbairn take […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 18: Houston Texans DE Derek Barnett (95) scoops up a fumble during game featuring the Houston Texans and the Dallas Cowboys on November 18, 2024 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, TX. (Photo by John Rivera/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images How are we here again? Your Houston Texans are 0-3. The offense, full of weapons, is struggling to put more than 18 points per game on the board and suddenly, this is a must-win match up against the Oklahoma South Cowboys. Fanduel ‘s odds currently have the Texans down by 3 . Will Kaimi Fairbairn take that bet and kick H-Town to their first win of 2026? Hopefully it won’t come to that. However, the betting site’s first prop bet has the Texans opening drive ending in a field goal as a more likely outcome than a touchdown. Texans fan and BRB faithful Sarlegant pointed out a recent Seth Payne video the other day where former H-Town defender Payne unpacks some Texans truths. After listening to head coach Demeco Ryans discuss the coaching staff, play calling and some other nifty tidbits in the video,, there is hope for Battle Red Nation! If you’re unfamiliar with Seth Payne, despite his humorous self-deprecation, he holds a very unique place in local Texans coverage. As a former player, highly intelligent student of the game and passionate Texans fan, Payne has unique access and insights into the organization, coaching, schemes and on-field results. When he breaks things down, you’ll likely learn something new, and chuckle more than once along the way. Reason for hope : the offense gets Nico Collins and Ed Ingram back this week. Dallas pulled off a newsworthy trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers this week to secure cornerback Joey Porter Jr., who may start this weekend. Cowboy fans think that’s fantastic. Texans fans remember Collins facing Porter in the playoffs last season. Prediction One: Nico Collins scores on Joey Porter Jr. While Collins did not have a stellar outing in the Texans 30-6 blowout of the Steelers in last season’s wild card, Nico is a “put the team on your back and win” kind of player. Sitting on the sidelines, watching his teammates struggle to move the ball and score points has him chomping at the bit. With Tank Dell still out, Jayden Higgins on IR and the tight ends serving as o-linemen, Collins will get quarterback C.J. Stroud’s attention early and often. Expect him to step up. Prediction Two: Will Anderson Jr. has 3 sack game. Much has been said about the “players only” meeting led by Anderson Jr. last week. While not every player on the defense seemed to respond against the Indianapolis Colts, it’s very clear Anderson Jr. is on a mission to win a Super Bowl, even if he has to do it all by himself. Dak Prescott has been sacked 3 times so far in 2026, but he’s yet to face a defense like Houston’s. With the need to hold the ball a little longer, his desire to scramble will rise. Derek Stingley Jr. had 2 breakups and an interception the last time these teams met and Prescott will remember. And with that memory, he opens himself up to pressure from Danielle Hunter, Sheldon Rankins, Jadeveon Clowney and Anderson Jr. Reason for hope: Despite Ryans’ recent insistence that offensive coordinator Nick Caley will continue to call the plays, Ryans low-key admits things are not working as they should. How does this play out heading into this weekend’s game? Hopefully other voices (Stroud, QB coach Jerry Shuplinski, Ryans) will speak into the play calling. This offense has the talent to perform, just not the way Caley seems to think they should. On paper the Cowboys seem like the better team so far in 2026. But they’ve not stood toe-to-toe with a team like Josh Allen’s Buffalo Bills. Houston has, and nearly won. Prediction Three: Dallas Cowboys 19 Houston Texans 31 The Texans are due for a breakout game. H-town football fanship is perpetually sailing through rough seas, but for every trough between waves, there’s a crest to keep us all hoping for more. The offense seems to suddenly click, the defense contributes a touchdown, and Dare Ogunbowale will reignite the special teams. Not only will the Texans take their first win of 2026, they’ll beat the spread doing it. Brought to you by Fanduel. Winning is undefeated. Texans fans, make every game a shared experience! title: Five Good Texans Questions with Blogging the Boys
summary: Like the Olympics, the battle with the interstate rivals comes every four years. It is never a disappointment because someone in the state is getting bragging rights. Fortunately, we have some consistency here at five questions and so I get to catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys yet again. It was good […]
full_text: Like the Olympics, the battle with the interstate rivals comes every four years. It is never a disappointment because someone in the state is getting bragging rights. Fortunately, we have some consistency here at five questions and so I get to catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys yet again. It was good catching up with him again. Like the Texans, the Cowboys suffered a disappointing loss late and that is where our conversation hegan. Battle Red Blog: The Cowboys are obviously coming off a tough loss overseas to the Ravens. Are you concerned about a hangover? David Haprin: At this point, I’m concerned about everything Dallas Cowboys. Well, maybe not their ability to throw the ball on offense, but outside of that, nothing has been really solid in Dallas. In the Ravens game, the biggest cause of the loss was HC Brian Schottenheimer, something he has admitted himself. His play-calling in certain situations was abysmal and he knows it. In a weird way, if you look at a lot of things that happened in that game, the Cowboys played pretty well, especially considering the amount of injuries they have on defense. They got their run game going, their defense had some splash plays that kept them in the game, but mistakes on the field, and especially along the sideline, really cost them. They were in position to beat the Ravens, and beat them pretty handily. But they threw it all away. Will there be a hangover from that? Maybe, one never knows with this team. BRB: The Cowboys offense has always been able to move the ball and score points. Are there any new wrinkles that fans from outside of Cowboys Nation might not be expecting? DH: I wouldn’t say much has changed since that part of the team went virtually untouched from last season. From the coaches, to the starters, even to some of the backups, it is a unit with a high continuity level. They will do what they do. They love to run Javonte Williams between the tackles. They will give a lot of eye candy pre-snap, and they use movement blocking from their offensive line in the run game in diverse ways, but essentially what they want is Williams chewing up yards between the tackles. That allows them the freedom to use their passing game, which is the star of the show in Dallas. Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens are the best thing Dallas has going for them. Outside of his playoff issues, Prescott is a stats machine. Lamb and Pickens can be used all over the field. Pickens is thought of as a deep ball, contested-catch specialist, but the Cowboys will throw a short slant to him also. Lamb can be used everywhere, even on screens. Backing them up are TE Jake Ferguson and WR3 Ryan Flournoy. As long as their offensive line holds up, they will score points. BRB: Obviously the Cowboys defense has been more shaky. What is the key for them getting back on track? DH: I mean, at this point, we are just hoping for performances where they hold the team in the game so the offense can win it. That usually means making a few splash plays in a game to create a turnover, a fourth-down stop, or something that gives the offense the ball in decent position. They don’t have a good pass rush, that is one of their problems. They are okay creating pressure, but they don’t get sacks. Mobile QBs also really hurt them. They are also not great against the run, although they did a decent job of keeping Derrick Henry in check last Sunday. Their biggest problem right now is the injuries in the secondary. The Cowboys defense has suffered an inordinate amount of injuries recently, with a large cluster in the secondary. We almost ran out of bodies back there against the Ravens. Rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham and rookie safety Caleb Downs have been the best players on that side of the ball. The Cowboys need some of their veterans, like Quinnen Williams, Rashan Gary and a few others to start playing up to their abilities to get close to back on track. BRB: Are there any key injuries that could have a significant impact on the game on Sunday? DH: Short answer – absolutely. Long answer – on offense, we are still without our best lineman in G Tyler Smith, but sub T.J. Bass has been great. On defense: Starting CB Cobie Durant has been out, and will likely miss this week, too. Starting LB DeMarvion Overshown has been out but it is possible he suits up this week. Starting S Malik Hooker has been out but he could also be back this week. Starting S Jalen Thompson was hurt in the Ravens game and is likely going to IR. Top backup CB Shavon Revel was hurt in the Ravens game and his status is unknown. Top backup S P.J. Locke has been put on IR. Backup DT Jonathan Bullard might go to IR. BRB: How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? DH: Honestly, I am so unsure this week. The Cowboys are Jekyll and Hyde, sometimes in the same game. We just never know how they will play. But it is early in the season and I am still an optimist, so I am going to take the Cowboys for the win, but it is going to be a close one. The Cowboys offense will move the ball, even against really good defenses they can usually generate some points, but their defense can make the most mediocre of offenses look all-world. In the end, I’m betting, speaking of prop bets, on the trio of Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. They will lead Dallas to a squeaker of a win. We wanted to thank David again for taking the time to answer our questions and for being so easy to work with again after four long seasons. We want to wish David and the Cowboys the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck begins on Monday morning.

title: Value of Things: By the Numbers
summary: It gets tougher to write these when you are 0-3, but looking at the numbers can help us figure out what could happen on Sunday. There are two struggling football teams meeting again which could mean the resistible force against the movable object. However, the rankings that we see will at least give us some […]
full_text: It gets tougher to write these when you are 0-3, but looking at the numbers can help us figure out what could happen on Sunday. There are two struggling football teams meeting again which could mean the resistible force against the movable object. However, the rankings that we see will at least give us some idea of what each team is thinking coming into Sunday. Obviously, the main story is a struggling offense against a struggling defense and a good offense against a good defense. However, we can break that down further by looking at the breakdown between rushing offense and passing offense along with rushing defense and passing defense. We are still early in the season, so some of these numbers may not mean anything when we get to week eighteen, but they are what we have right now. Texans Cowboys Rushing Yards 30th 23rd Passing Yards 10th 12th Rushing Yards Allowed 5th 31st Passing Yards Allowed 26th 14th Two weeks in a row the Texans are going against a bad defense. The Cowboys are 30th overall in yards allowed. They have surrendered 82 points which is 25th in the league in points allowed. This is a bad defense to be sure. However, even though the Texans are 14th in total yards gained they are 24th in points scored. That makes them one of the least efficient offenses in football. How will the Cowboys offense attack the Texans? At a certain point, you stop worrying about what other teams do well and look at what your team does well. The Cowboys have the most explosive receiver duo in football with Ceedee Lamb and George Pickens. Dak Prescrott is a top ten quarterback and some ambitious Prescott fans would say he is in the top five. At a certain point you stop worrying about what other teams do well and worry about what your team does well. The Cowboys pass the football as good as any team. They don’t run the ball well, so it really shouldn’t matter whether the Texans defend the run well or not. However, they happen to defend it well, so they have more than one reason to rely on their passing game. What will the Cowboys defense plan to do to the Texans? This one is easy. You shut down the run and make the Texans one-dimensional. Fortunately for the Texans, the Cowboys pass rush is the weakness of their defense. So, you have a bad defensive line against a bad offensive line. This will be the matchup of the season and it could very well decide which of these teams have a chance from this week forward. The Texans are likely out if they go to 0-4 and the Cowboys chances are limited if they go to 1-3. What will the Texans offense do to the Cowboys defense? How long do we have? There is what you plan to do and what you actually end up doing. The Texans keep telling everyone they are a running team and through three weeks they have been anything but. This has been going on for years as even when they had Joe Mixon they were not really a good running team. The important thing comes when a team finally realizes what their identity is. Maybe this will be the week that the Texans finally admit who they are and who they aren’t. I’m not sure if this will be the week. Maybe some heads will have to roll before they finally get the picture. This is not a running football team. The sooner they admit this the better off we are all going to be. What will the Texans defense do to the Cowboys offense? If the game goes according to plan then the Cowboys will be a one-dimensional football team. This feels like a game where there will be explosive plays on both sides. So, the winning team likely is the one that will have the most explosives in this matchup. Will the Texans generate more rurnovers and negative plays than the Cowboys offense produce explosives on the positive end? In week one they didn’t, but they have at least broken even the last two weeks, so there is reason to believe they will bust out and make enough big plays with an interception or sack fumble.

It’s just endemic of terrible leadership. And, Demeco is a solid leader. Which begs the question: what is happening behind closed doors? Rumors of division in the team, the defense having “players only” meetings already? Not a good look, no matter how you slice it. Losing hurts all, winning heals. And the offense is not playing to win. Blame the Houston Texans General Manager? And, before the Caserio haters chime in and blame him for not drafting/signing/trading for better offensive lineman to give Caley more to work with, here’s an all-too familiar story: Lions C Juice Scruggs is currently the 4th-highest graded center (71.4) in the NFL, per PFF. pic.twitter.com/Tnna3qVU8v — 𝔗𝔥𝔢 𝔇𝔢𝔱𝔯𝔬𝔦𝔱 𝔗𝔦𝔪𝔢𝔰 📰 (@the_det_times) September 28, 2026 These are all NFL quality athletes. Caserio didn’t draft guys from the local Buffalo Wild Wings, he drafted highly rated, highly scouted, deeply researched collegiate athletes. They play under Caley (and Slowik) and stink. They move to other teams and do well. That leaves the door open to blame the scheme. The Erhardt-Perkins offensive is one of the best in the modern NFL. The scheme works and has worked in many places, earning an awful lot of Super Bowl trophies and rings. Hence, it’s not the GM, or the scheme. That leaves the offensive coaching staff: Caley, Popovich, et al.. Dallas Cowboys vs Houston Texans Which brings us to this week’s poll: Losing to Jerry’s Kids is worse than starting 0-3, especially when it leads to 0-4. Unfortunately, as long as Caley is calling the shots on offense, this team will continue to under-perform. The defense isn’t firing on all cylinders either, but that’s a topic for another post…

title: Bengals Injuries Create Major Opportunity for Jaguars in Week 4
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars head on the road in Week 4 to face off against the Cincinnati Bengals. Both teams enter Sunday’s Week 4 matchup in reasonably sound health at the star level. However, a few significant Cincinnati roster moves this week have reshuffled the Bengals’ depth chart in ways that could meaningfully change how this […]
full_text: Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen smiles while answering questions during a press conference after the seventh organized team activity at the Miller Electric Center in Jacksonville, Fla. Monday, June 2, 2025. [Doug Engle/Florida Times-Union] | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Jacksonville Jaguars head on the road in Week 4 to face off against the Cincinnati Bengals. Both teams enter Sunday’s Week 4 matchup in reasonably sound health at the star level. However, a few significant Cincinnati roster moves this week have reshuffled the Bengals’ depth chart in ways that could meaningfully change how this game unfolds. Bengals injury report includes a limited for DJ Turner. Will know more tomorrow, but would not have thought anything was wrong seeing him in the locker room. Battle and Cook continue on the limited track. pic.twitter.com/M3mIfYd8iw — Paul Dehner Jr. (@pauldehnerjr) October 1, 2026 Here is the full injury breakdown from Thursday’s injury report. Bengals Roster Shuffling CB Jalen Davis – Injured Reserve (Hamstring) Cincinnati placed starting slot cornerback Jalen Davis on Injured Reserve on Tuesday following the hamstring injury suffered during the Week 3 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Davis earned the starting nickelback role entering the season and was the veteran anchor of a cornerback room that was already operating without significant depth. He will miss Sunday, though he is eligible to return no earlier than Week 8. Davis to IR Impacts Backup slot cornerback Ja’Sir Taylor was drafted this year and viewed as insurance behind Davis, and was placed on Injured Reserve coming out of training camp and isn’t eligible to return until next week. Bengals defensive coordinator Al Golden confirmed that outside starting cornerback Dax Hill would be moving back into the slot corner role. Hill has played at every level of Cincinnati’s secondary across his career, since entering the league as a first-round pick in 2022. In his rookie year, he was deployed at free safety, then box safety, then slot cornerback, before eventually settling as an outside corner over the last two seasons. While his versatility could help Cincinnati in the slot, shuffling their best remaining cornerback inside creates an opening on the outside that Cincinnati doesn’t have a proven answer for. The outside cornerback spot Hill vacates will likely go to DJ Ivey, though 2026 third-round pick rookie Tacario Davis has been getting increased snaps as of late, and multiple Cincinnati media members believe the team could use some combination of both players Sunday. In a game where Jacksonville is deploying four legitimate receiving threats across multiple positions, whichever of the two lines up across from that group becomes an immediate priority target. Put plainly: when the Bengals operate in nickel, Cincinnati’s CB4 or CB5 from the start of the season will now be receiving starting snaps. That’s a significant vulnerability against a Jacksonville receiving room operating with full health and confidence following the 35-6 performance against New England. These moves could also force Cincinnati to adjust how they deploy their defensive structure, moving away from nickel looks or coverages they would normally run with more experienced personnel. WR Andrei Iosivas – Injured Reserve (Thumb) & WR Colbie Young – TBD (Knee) Cincinnati’s receiving room has taken its own share of attrition. Iosivas, the team’s third wideout, was placed on Injured Reserve following Week 2, and his replacement Young, seems unlikely to suit up Sunday after suffering a hip-drop tackle last week and not practicing on Wednesday or Thursday. The assumption in most circles is that tight end Mike Gesicki could absorb additional target volume as the third receiving option in Cincinnati’s offense with both players unavailable. The Bengals did re-sign wide receiver Mitch Tinsley this week as part of their roster adjustments, and Dohnte Meyers is listed on the updated depth chart as the top slot receiver. Jaguars fans may recognize Tinsley as the receiver who hauled in a one-handed, 13-yard touchdown against Jarrian Jones from Jake Browning last season, his only catch of that game, but an exceptional individual play. His re-addition to the active roster gives Cincinnati another option in the event their receiving depth is tested further. TOUCHDOWN ABSURDO DO MITCHELL TINSLEY! 😱😱 pic.twitter.com/urDnDkUQc5 — NFL Brasil (@NFLBrasil) September 14, 2025 RG Dalton Risner – TBD (Knee) The most significant offensive injury to monitor heading into Sunday concerns Bengals starting right guard Dalton Risner. Risner didn’t practice Wednesday or Thursday and was still wearing a brace on his right knee during individual work on the rehab field, despite telling reporters Monday that he expected to be fine. Friday’s practice designation will be the clearest signal of whether he plays. Risner has been one of the more productive guards in pass protection this season, ranking among the top ten at his position in successful pass block rate, per Pro Football Focus. More specifically, he’s the lineman Cincinnati routinely leaves to block on an island on the right side, which allows them to focus additional help toward left guard Dylan Fairchild, who they rarely leave in one-on-one situations. Could be a big loss for Bengals deep passing game if RG Dalton Risner can't go. Jalen Rivers would start Risner is a quality pass blocker who's trusted on an island vs a 2nd year Rivers (16 games w/ 7 starts in 2025, 27 pressures, 2 sacks, 4 QB hits allowed, & 1 flag in 2025) https://t.co/DWSACK3GrY — 𝕋𝕣𝕒𝕧𝕚𝕤 🅓. ℍ𝕠𝕝𝕞𝕖𝕤 (@TravisDHolmes) October 1, 2026 Losing Risner could force Cincinnati to redistribute that pass protection, either leaving Fairchild more exposed or adding additional help via running back chipping or tight end assistance. This bears close attention on Friday’s final injury report. Jaguars Holding Steady Jacksonville is in roughly the same health position they carried into Week 3 against the Denver Broncos, which is to say they are among the healthier rosters in the AFC. The only notable development this week was tight end Nate Boerkircher missing Thursday’s practice with an illness. In addition to Boerkircher, the official Thursday injury report listed the following players as limited: RB LeQuint Allen (hip) DT DaVon Hamilton (back) WR Jakobi Meyers (thumb) DT Albert Regis (elbow) CB Christian Braswell (knee) CB Montaric Brown (hamstring) RT Cole Van Lanen (knee) Cornerback Jarrian Jones, who entered the week listed with a hip designation, was a full participant for the second consecutive day, an encouraging sign ahead of a matchup against Cincinnati’s elite receiving corps. The Bigger Picture The week’s most consequential injury developments belong entirely to Cincinnati. Losing Jalen Davis and Colbie Young in the same week, compounding Iosivas’ earlier IR placement, has left the Bengals navigating their passing game and secondary with considerably less depth than they likely anticipated entering the season. For Jacksonville, a receiving room that features Parker Washington, Jakobi Meyers, Brian Thomas Jr., Josh Cameron, and Brenton Strange has every reason to view Sunday’s matchup as a genuine opportunity to impose their identity against a cornerback group operating well below full strength. Friday’s final injury report, particularly Risner’s status, will determine the final shape of this matchup. But the direction of the injury news this week has pointed consistently toward Jacksonville. Sunday’s Week 4 road matchup between the Jaguars and Bengals is scheduled for 1 p.m. EST.

title: 5 Questions with Cincy Jungle: Don’t Forget About Tee Higgins
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4, we exchanged questions with Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Excluding QB and WR, which Bengals position group gives you the most confidence? Excluding LB, which unit worries you most? Oddly enough, given the resources […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, CA - SEPTEMBER 14: Tee Higgins #5 of the Cincinnati Bengals and Trevor Lawrence #16 of the Jacksonville Jaguars embrace prior to an NFL game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on September 14, 2025 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4, we exchanged questions with Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Excluding QB and WR, which Bengals position group gives you the most confidence? Excluding LB, which unit worries you most? Oddly enough, given the resources thrown at the position, defensive tackle has become a strength once again. The trade for Dexter Lawrence and the acquisition of Jonathan Allen have reverberated through the team on a number of levels. Aside from the rest of the team sensing the “all-in” mentality from a hyper-aggressive offseason (at least by this team’s standards), these two have brought locker room leadership and on-field production. Last year’s IDL starters, T.J. Slaton Jr. and B.J. Hill (both still good players), are now rotational guys, which makes this front formidable, as it was back in 2021 when they had Hill, DJ Reader, Larry Ogunjobi and others on the inside. Many on the outside looking in will readily point to the offensive line as a concern, but this is a solid (albeit flawed) unit. For this week in particular, I’m concerned about the safety position. Free agent acquisition Bryan Cook is nursing an injury, while hybrid guy Kyle Dugger is ailing as well. If it’s PJ Jules and Jordan Battle as the main safeties this week, play Trevor Lawrence in your fantasy league. Get ready for game day with SB Nation’s new app! SB Nation’s NEW game chat feature in the app is perfect for keeping the latest Jaguars updates and conversations at your fingertips. With a couple of clicks you can visit Dawgs By Nature and learn everything you need to know about this week’s opponent! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 2: How has the offseason addition of Dexter Lawrence changed Cincinnati’s defense? He’s brought work ethic, increased accountability, and a “have fun playing ball” mentality. He’s also backed it up on the field. While he wasn’t heavily in the stat column in Weeks 1 and 2, he showed up in a big way, statistically speaking. He freed up others to make plays–particularly in the two wins. His size, and overall ability to impact the pass and run game can’t be denied. Lawrence hovers around 60% of defensive snaps taken through the first three games, but he is incredibly effective, and has allowed Al Golden to unleash a potent rotation. Running up the middle has been largely stymied, but space plays have still hurt the Bengals (your comments about the linebackers). Question 3: What have you learned about the 2026 Bengals through three weeks that you wouldn’t have guessed before the season? I’ve learned that this team has urgency, but similar flaws to what we’ve seen from late 2023 through 2025. Additional talent, leadership, and Championship mindsets have been added to this roster. But, I think it’s unknown if this team can get beyond the 9-10-win threshold that we have seen from seasons in which Joe Burrow is healthy. The 2-0 start revved a lot of people up, but a frustratingly familiar loss to the AFC North bullies, the Pittsburgh Steelers, brought up more questions. Can they beat the teams outside of the division with some sort of regularity? Sure. Can they get 4-5 wins in the AFC North and get through the gauntlet of the playoffs? I think most people want more to be seen. Question 4: Who is one player you’re expecting to have a good game, and one player you’re hoping to have a good game? Tee Higgins has quietly been exceptional, although under the radar. Between his pass-catching and run-blocking prowess, he has been silently amazing. But, with how things have been on offense, and the heavy reliance on him, kicker Evan McPherson needs to continue to be amazing. Those are expected ones. In terms of hoping a player has a big game, I’d say either Cashius Howell and/or Shemar Stewart. The former (the team’s first pick in the 2026 draft after the Lawrence trade) has been a spark plug, while the latter has been injured and has an odd pro trajectory, to say the least. Question 5: Do you expect the Bengals to cover as 2.5-point favorites, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game? I think the Jags have either a decently comfortable win, and/or the Bengals barely cover. I think this Bengals team is talented, but I still think they are trying to figure things out. Look at the non-obvious guys to make waves this week, for both teams. Higgins, Tuten, Chase Brown, etc. Thanks to Anthony for taking the time to answer our questions. title: Jaguars vs. Bengals: Matchup History Through the Decades
summary: After a spectacular performance at home against the New England Patriots, the Jacksonville Jaguars are back on the road in Cincinnati this week. The former AFC Central Division rivals have played each other 26 times, and the series is currently tied. Jimmy Smith said the Jags are going to beat the Bengals’ asses, so let’s look […]
full_text: 09 Dec 2001 : Rich Braham #74 of the Cincinnati Bengals faces the Jacksonville Jaguars during the game at Paul Brown Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio. The Jaguars won 14-10. DIGITAL IMAGE. Mandatory Credit : Tom Pidgeon/Allsport | Getty Images After a spectacular performance at home against the New England Patriots, the Jacksonville Jaguars are back on the road in Cincinnati this week. The former AFC Central Division rivals have played each other 26 times , and the series is currently tied. Jimmy Smith said the Jags are going to beat the Bengals’ asses, so let’s look back at the Jaguars doing exactly that on the Bengals’ home turf through the decades. The 1990’s Week 8 on October 31, 1999 Final score: Jaguars 41 – Bengals 10 Attendance: 49,138 I figured an October win would be the best way to start this. During 30:01 of possession, the Jaguars recorded 23 first downs and 377 total net yards. Defensive dominance led to touchdowns from Fred Taylor, Keenan McCardell, Jimmy Smith, and two field goals from Mike Hollis, being the only points scored during the first half.
