title: The Seahawks are being heavily blitzed, and it’s part of a greater NFL trend
summary: If it feels like the Seattle Seahawks offense has faced a lot of extra pressure, your eyes are not deceiving you. Through three games, Seahawks opponents have blitzed on 43.4% of pass plays (according to NFL Pro/NextGenStats), good for second-highest rate in the NFL behind the Chicago Bears. It’s probably not a coincidence that the […]
full_text: If it feels like the Seattle Seahawks offense has faced a lot of extra pressure, your eyes are not deceiving you. Through three games, Seahawks opponents have blitzed on 43.4% of pass plays ( according to NFL Pro/NextGenStats ), good for second-highest rate in the NFL behind the Chicago Bears. It’s probably not a coincidence that the Chicago Bears are first and the Green Bay Packers are fourth, as those teams have already felt the wrath of the Minnesota Vikings and Brian Flores’ blitz-a-palooza. Seattle, meanwhile, has faced two of the top five blitzing defenses in the Washington Commanders and New England Patriots. Even the Arizona Cardinals, who rank near the bottom in blitz rate, blitzed Drew Lock above their season average. This isn’t anything new for the Seahawks, who faced the third-highest blitz rate last season on their way to winning the Super Bowl. What is different is how they’re getting blitzed, and it’s something of a growing trend across the NFL. JP Acosta, a wonderful SB Nation alum who now works for CBS Sports, recently penned a fascinating column examining a league-wide trend among defensive coordinators . As more teams shift toward under-center plays (usually with 12 and 13 personnel), DCs are just blitzing the hell out of those looks. If you digest football online, you’ve probably heard this before: “everyone in the NFL is going under center now,” and it’s true. Across the league, NFL teams are going under center to manufacture their offense at a rate we haven’t seen this decade. According to TruMedia, through Week 3, the under-center rate is 42.0%, the highest the league has seen since 2013. If we want to parse it further, on early downs (first and second down), 2026’s 49.6% under-center rate is also the highest since 2013. Even with the higher under-center frequency, the leaguewide success rate under center (47.4%) is also the highest it’s been in that same time period (2025 is second at 46.9%). Teams are returning to ethical football, leaving behind the shotgun/RPO world we thought we’d get after the iconic Rams-Chiefs shootout of 2018. But how are defenses countering the return to the under-center game that offenses are throwing at them? Longtime college defensive coordinator Don Brown once said to “solve your problems with aggression,” and NFL defenses have taken note. The leaguewide blitz rate against all under-center passes is 51% through three weeks, the highest the NFL has seen since TruMedia started tracking blitz rate in 2006. Teams are leaning into the aggression to cause chaotic plays, but the reason why is a great illustration of the constant battle for supremacy within the white lines. The Seahawks are one of only a handful of teams that runs the majority of their offense from under-center , so they are ripe for the counter-blitz revolution. Seattle also runs play-action at the second-highest clip in the NFL, which is another relevant data point: Opposing defenses are blitzing under-center play action passes at a 52% clip through three games, the highest rate TruMedia has ever tracked. Over 60 percent of Seattle’s under-center dropbacks have been blitzed. Based on NFL Pro tracking, they were blitzed less than half the time from under-center dropbacks in 2025. What is notable, however, is that offensive coordinator Brian Fleury has yet to establish an under-center pass game without play-action. There have only been two non-PA attempts out of 32 under-center dropbacks, one of which was the tying touchdown to Jaxon Smith-Njigba against the New England Patriots. For comparison, the San Francisco 49ers have 15 non-PA passes out of 30 UC dropbacks. With essentially two games of Drew Lock and only one with Darnold (who didn’t have a single non-PA UC pass against the Washington Commanders), it might be too early to declare any tendencies for Fleury, but it wouldn’t make much sense for a Shanahan disciple to only want to use play-action passing from under center. None of this is necessarily bad, by the way. It’s a defensive counter to a change in offensive strategies, as is the nature of sport. If there’s good news to glean from these three weeks, it’s the fact that Drew Lock and Sam Darnold have both shredded the blitz (from UC, shotgun, and pistol) to the combined tune of 30/41 for 382 yards, 3 TDs, 0 INTs, and only two sacks taken. Seattle’s EPA/pass against the blitz ranks third in the NFL behind the San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs. JP’s column did dive into defenses using blitzing to combat the proliferation of outside zone runs, which would definitely be relevant to the Seahawks. The only thing I’ll add is that Seattle is still dealing with one of the highest stacked box rates in the NFL at 32.2%. I don’t have the data for run blitz rate, but the Seahawks run game has performed poorly by EPA/play against stacked boxes, so Seattle is having to deal with a steady diet of loading up to stop the run while sending extra pressure to deal with the heavier personnel, under-center looks. Regardless of whether it’s under center, shotgun, or pistol, one thing is clear: DCs are blitzing more, full stop. Across the league, blitz rates are skyrocketing. The 32.3% leaguewide blitz rate is the highest in the NFL since 2010, but it’s not all emotional blitzing after a big play. These are calculated moves, schematic tweaks to force offenses out of their under-center comfort zone and swing the odds back in their favor. …Well, except the Seahawks, who rank 31st in blitz rate. We’ll see if that changes any time soon once the secondary is healthy again.

title: All-22 review: The good and bad from the Seahawks loss to the Commanders
summary: The Seattle Seahawks entered Week 3 after two wins to open the season, but the Washington Commanders exposed some of the problems that had been hidden during those first two weeks. The Seahawks still moved the ball well (only in the air), finishing with 437 total yards and 28 first downs while averaging 6.8 yards […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks entered Week 3 after two wins to open the season, but the Washington Commanders exposed some of the problems that had been hidden during those first two weeks. The Seahawks still moved the ball well (only in the air), finishing with 437 total yards and 28 first downs while averaging 6.8 yards per play. Sam Darnold threw for 379 yards and four touchdowns, while Jaxon Smith-Njigba continued his ridiculous start to the season with 10 catches for 128 yards and two touchdowns. But none of that was enough in the end. Seattle turned the ball over three times, with those mistakes producing 21 points for Washington. The Seahawks also struggled badly to run the ball, gave up several critical plays on defense and once again had issues on special teams. The Commanders finished with just 258 total yards, but Marcus Mariota and Washington’s offense made enough plays late to escape with a 33-31 win. So, for the first time this season, let’s take a look at what worked and what went wrong in a loss. The Bad The run game was completely neutralized There is plenty of blame to go around here. Seattle finished with just 44 rushing yards on 18 attempts, a miserable 2.4 yards per carry. The offensive line struggled to create movement consistently, the running backs didn’t always find the available lanes, and the play-calling didn’t do enough to manufacture positive runs. Clear example of one of many OL mistakes. On this outside zone, Grey Zabel must reach the 1-tech. He loses the block, forcing the RB outside into the defender who beat Abe Lucas for a 4-yard loss. Not sure if Lucas expected Barner's help. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-01T00:02:34.389Z Here’s a clear example of one of the many mistakes along the offensive line. This is an outside zone run to the right, and Grey Zabel is supposed to execute a reach block on the 1-technique defender. It’s a difficult block, but a crucial one for the concept, and Zabel has already executed it brilliantly several times this season. He loses the block here, forcing the running back to bounce outside, where he runs directly into the defender who beat Abe Lucas for a four-yard loss. I’m not sure if Lucas was expecting help from AJ Barner before the tight end worked to his block, but the angle is poor and Lucas can’t recover. We saw plenty of mistakes like this throughout the game. It was a recurring theme: two offensive linemen would execute their blocks well, while someone else would miss his assignment and turn the play into a significant loss. The running back situation was also a factor. Price fumbled and, rightfully so, he was put in the doghouse afterward. However, Seattle needs to find a way to get its first-round running back on the field, and the running back also needs to stop putting the ball on the ground. Emmanuel Wilson deserves some blame too. title: Our first month with an app broke our commenting records
summary: A month ago we announced the release of our new app, which you can find here or by searching SB Nation in your neighborhood app store. Quite a few of you have downloaded it over the past month and have been using it.  The goal with this app was to make it easier to join […]
full_text: (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images A month ago we announced the release of our new app, which you can find here or by searching SB Nation in your neighborhood app store. Quite a few of you have downloaded it over the past month and have been using it. The goal with this app was to make it easier to join the community, and specifically comment, read the comments, and make your own posts, as well as keeping all the community posts – articles on the front page, Feed posts from you – front and center. The results so far are encouraging. In fact, it’s helped us set a new all-time record for comments this month across all of SB Nation’s communities, and I want to thank you for that. One of the most exciting new features is the game chat. It makes it easier to follow along with the barrage of comments that come during games and gets to the heart of why so many of you spend time in our community. Faster loading comments and notifications when someone replies to your comments and Feed posts are creating a more fun experience that you’re not going to find anywhere else. We also wanted to elevate the community’s contributions by putting your Feed posts inside one stream alongside all the other articles from the site. To that end, more people have seen your posts and more people have commented on them. In fact, we’ve set single-day commenting records three different times since the season started. And if you prefer just reading our traditional front page articles, there’s an option at the top to do that. So, one month in, thanks for making us part of your routine. If you haven’t checked it out, you can get it for iOs or Android . And if you’re not an app user, that’s OK! We’re glad to have you following along in whatever way makes you most comfortable.

title: Where the 49ers have surprised the most through three weeks
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are off to a hot 3-0 start to the 2026 season, securing wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, and Arizona Cardinals. So far, it’s been their offense that’s been the story, as the 49ers have excelled behind Brock Purdy, playing mistake-free football and ranking first in the NFL (by […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - SEPTEMBER 20: Offensive tackle Trent Williams (71) of the San Francisco 49ers in action against the Miami Dolphins during a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are off to a hot 3-0 start to the 2026 season, securing wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, and Arizona Cardinals. So far, it’s been their offense that’s been the story, as the 49ers have excelled behind Brock Purdy, playing mistake-free football and ranking first in the NFL (by far) in EPA per play. Their passing offense has especially come out strong, as Purdy looks like an MVP candidate, but we’re also slowly starting to see the run game built out with Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black. It isn’t a surprise that the 49ers offense has looked good. Many have under Kyle Shanahan, but this unit has looked quite elite through three weeks, and it isn’t just Purdy and the skill position players. The offensive line has also played quite well, holding up in pass protection, while the run blocking is also starting to play out. According to Ben Baldwin’s formula, which takes into account PFF grades, blown block percentage, and pass-block win rate, the 49ers rank first in the NFL in pass protection rankings currently. Pass protection ratings pic.twitter.com/l4WuVTlpW7 — Computer Cowboy (@benbbaldwin) September 29, 2026 They lead the NFL in both PFF grades and blown block percentage through three weeks, and they also haven’t given up a sack. What has the coaching staff seen from that unit so far? “I think they’ve been really good,” offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. “We knew who four out of the five would be, I think, in general, but as far as the guard competition, we felt really good. Whoever ended up starting was going to be the right guy and play good for us. These guys have done a heck of a job through three weeks. Obviously, no sacks, but I look at that as a team stat too. “It has a lot to do with, obviously, the O-Line, our tight ends, our backs, our quarterback, our receivers being in the right place. There’s been a little bit of luck involved. Brock’s made some great plays of making people miss. So, it’s really a team stat. It has to do with our offense being efficient and staying on track, and so far so good. Hope to keep that going.” The 49ers are also bringing back that efficiency in the run game after struggling last season. So far, they’re averaging 5.1 yards per carry as a team, with Christian McCaffrey up at 4.7 yards per carry on 35 attempts. What has been the key to being more efficient there? “I felt like we were really efficient running the ball, staying out of long passing situations, second and long, third and long,” Kubiak added. “In this game, it felt like maybe in the second half we got that going a little bit more. Anytime you can be efficient on first down running the ball, it’s going to help. I always talk about staying out of obvious passing situations where the D-Line can tee off, where a play caller might change up their coverages. It just gets harder when you’re in those situations, so the more efficient we can be. “I’ve been real happy with our backs. They’ve had some good runs, but there’s been hard runs that get us four, five, six yards that maybe were blocked for three that keep us on track, get us to second and four and then maybe third and two and we have a better chance of staying on the field. Then you look at the second half last week, Christian [McCaffrey] had a 12-yard run in the fourth quarter. That’s what we’re talking about. Those just efficient grinder runs that keep you on the field and let you keep calling plays, so hopefully we keep that going.” So far, when it comes to protection, Jake Brendel has allowed just one pressure through 163 pass-blocking reps. Dominick Puni has given up just two, while Connor Colby and Colton McKivitz have given up four each, and Trent Williams has allowed five. The 49ers offensive line was a strength last season as well, but the run game never really got going. Now, that unit is looking like a strength again this season, and they’re near the top of the NFL in a couple of metrics so far.

title: 49ers News: Dante Pettis redemption game loading?
summary: I was looking at PFF grades and noticed some interesting things about the Broncos’ performance against the Rams. Of course, you have to take PFF grades with a grain of salt, but I found it interesting that….  The Broncos are the most formidable opponent yet but they’re gettable, especially on the ground. So excited for […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - DECEMBER 9: Dante Pettis #18 of the San Francisco 49ers runs after making a reception during the game against the Denver Broncos at Levi's Stadium on December 9, 2018 in Santa Clara, California. The 49ers defeated the Broncos 20-14. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images I was looking at PFF grades and noticed some interesting things about the Broncos’ performance against the Rams. Of course, you have to take PFF grades with a grain of salt, but I found it interesting that…. Lineback Justin Strnad had a decent pass coverage grade, which I initially pegged as a weakness of the Broncos. Patrick Surtain II had the worst game of his career against Davante Adams (just wait til he sees Dante Pettis) Riley Moss was also a liability on the back end for their defense. Bo Nix was the lowest rated player on offense. The Broncos are the most formidable opponent yet but they’re gettable, especially on the ground. So excited for this match-up. 49ers Week 3 Trench Grades: Throwing bodies at the problem (paywall) “Shout out Sebastian Valdez, who I mentioned in yesterday’s tape takeaways. They used him in just about everything but a wide-nine role, and he was impressive in the run game. I also feel like Osa probably should have been lower here, but I gave some deference to the fact that he faced a ton of double teamed and while he wasn’t all that impressive, he had a lot of Dom Puni-esque survivor reps. I’ll tend to give guys credit for holding up long enough to occupy two defenders, even if they get displaced later in the rep. Some (not to say the majority, just some) “good” reps might just allow a linebacker to fill and stay clean, even if that player eventually looks to have lost the rep. It’s like how you can have a sack, but if you’re completely unblocked, I’m not counting that as a very good rep…. …..I was pleasantly surprised with Khalid Kareem’s day, though a lot of that came against Cardinals RT Elijah Wilkinson. He’s terrible. Osa’s grade ended up higher than I expected. I thought Keion White was probably the 49ers’ best pass rusher in this game, but most of their pressures came off blitzes and simulated pressures. Kevin Givens also had a few nice reps….Colton McKivitz was downright imperious this week. I thought Trent Williams underwhelmed in pass protection before leaving the game. He got attacked at his inside hip effectively a few times….Now, in the run game? Trent was magnificent. I legitimately enjoy watching him attack a linebacker in space more than anything else the 49ers do.” How 49ers’ Fred Warner learned to stop worrying and embrace the hunt (paywall) “There were little things going on physically early on and I was just not playing like myself,” Warner said. “But then I had people in my ear asking, ‘Hey, do you feel like you’re trying to do too much because of the contract? ’ I truly did not think that was the case. But once that got in my head, I started thinking about that … “I developed this sense of urgency for me to make that play that would validate me making the money I was making. And then you start reaching to try to do things and that really puts you behind the 8-ball. It just all started to snowball.” Before the 2021 season, Warner had already devoured books such as “Mind Gym: An Athlete’s Guide to Inner Excellence”; “12 Rules for Life: An Antidote to Chaos”; “Atomic Habits: Tiny Changes, Remarkable Results” and, of course, “Kobe Bryant: The Mamba Mentality.” “Those tools I’d learned had really helped me get to a spot where I was really being successful,” Warner said. “But then once I let the negative thoughts flood my brain, there was no getting out of that. I knew about controlling the controllables. Keeping things simple. But that was all gone. I was so in my head with all the other stuff. I needed someone to bring me back into focus.” …..“My first thought when I talked with Fred was that he was a great player who started thinking too much about being a great player,” Afremow said. “Suddenly, every play, every moment in every game, started to feel like he wanted to provide evidence: ‘Am I still that guy? Am I living up to this? ’ … He needed to stop making every play a referendum on whether he was still Fred Warner.” Afremow’s charge: Remind Warner “who the hell he already was.” The question that unlocked it is surprising: What animal do you most identify with? “And I’m like ‘Oh, of course, the lion. That’s the king of the jungle. There’s the hair, the mane,’” Warner said, touching his dreadlocks. “It just made too much sense.” Afremow agreed. And he kept asking questions: If a lion goes out on a hunt and doesn’t get a kill, does that mean it’s not a lion? The answer was obvious. For Warner, the deeper meaning was transformative. His inability to get interceptions or forced fumbles didn’t make him less Fred Warner. The stats would come. “The thing that a lion does, they don’t have to think about it, they just hunt,” Warner said. “And I just needed to get back to loving the hunt. I was focused on outcomes and things that were out of my control. “Jim was like, ‘Why don’t you just focus on the hunt and get back to things that made you who you are? What made you the lion, what made you Fred? ’ … That truly saved my entire career. Ever since, I’ve gone out there with the mentality of ‘hunt’ and let everything else come as it may.” …Warner felt freedom after his breakthrough, but he also worried: What did it say about his mindset if he’d allowed negative thoughts to consume him? Was he weak or, worse, broken? Afremow’s answer: He was human. “It’s being able to understand: This is how we’re built,” Afremow said. “We all have a protective voice that says, ‘Hey, are you ready for this? Can you do this? What if it doesn’t work out? ’ We don’t have to take our first thought at face value. So for Fred, it was acknowledging and validating: ‘Of course you’re going to have negative thoughts at times. What you’re experiencing makes total sense.’” Once-dismissed 49ers WR Dante Pettis is back. They might need him Sunday (paywall) “ If both can’t play Sunday, the only healthy receivers on the active roster would be Deebo Samuel, Jacob Cowing and Jordan Watkins. Because they need at least five receivers on game days, practice squad players Pettis and Brandin Cooks could be elevated. Pettis, 30, hasn’t started a game since 2022 with the Chicago Bears. Last year he caught nine passes for 127 yards for the New Orleans Saints. If he’s in uniform against the Broncos, the first three players the 49ers drafted in 2018 — Broncos tackle Mike McGlinchey, Pettis and linebacker Fred Warner (a third-round pick) — will be on hand. Two others from that draft class, defensive tackle Kentavius Street (a fourth-rounder with the Bears) and cornerback D.J. Reed (a fifth-rounder now with the Detroit Lions), remain in the league.” 49ers QB Brock Purdy named NFC Offensive Player of the Month “Purdy is the only quarterback with multiple touchdown passes and a passer rating of at least 100 in each of the first three weeks of the season.” John Lynch on Mike Evans: ‘Mike’s going to make every attempt to try to play’ “The 49ers must’ve felt like Nick Bosa was closer to “week-to-week” since they didn’t place him on Injured Reserve. Bosa pulled his calf muscle in practice last week, missing Week 3.”

title: 49ers elevate Brandin Cooks to active roster after WR released on Thursday
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are elevating veteran wide receiver Brandin Cooks from the practice squad to the active roster, while also bringing back wideout Malik Turner to the practice squad. ESPN’s Nick Wagoner reported that Khadarel Hodge, who has been dealing with a knee injury this week, was not seen at the beginning of Thursday’s […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 17: Brandin Cooks #18 of the Buffalo Bills goes up for the ball during an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are elevating veteran wide receiver Brandin Cooks from the practice squad to the active roster, while also bringing back wideout Malik Turner to the practice squad. ESPN’s Nick Wagoner reported that Khadarel Hodge, who has been dealing with a knee injury this week, was not seen at the beginning of Thursday’s practice. The 49ers announced they released Hodge shortly after. Cooks, who just turned 33 last week, was signed to the practice squad after the 49ers dealt with several injuries at wide receiver. The 49ers entered the season without Ricky Pearsall and Christian Kirk and have since lost De’Zhaun Stribling and Demarcus Robinson. Now, Khadarel Hodge, who was signed to the active roster two weeks ago after being on the practice squad, is no longer on the team. In addition, Mike Evans is currently dealing with a rib injury, leaving the 49ers with Deebo Samuel, Jacob Cowing, and Jordan Watkins as their other healthy receivers. Hodge got a big step up in work without Demarcus Robinson in the fold, playing 30 of 54 snaps against the Arizona Cardinals. That was only behind Deebo Samuel among receivers. Now, the 49ers could look to Cooks, who signed last week, to fill the void on the perimeter, as they scrounge for more depth. Cooks, who is just 189 receiving yards away from 10,000 career yards, played 15 games between the New Orleans Saints and Buffalo Bills last season. He caught 24 passes for 279 yards, while adding five catches and 78 yards in two playoff games for the Bills. Malik Turner has been a mainstay with the 49ers in the offseason for the last few years. He was in training camp with the team in 2024 and played on the practice squad that season. He was with the team on the practice squad all of last season as well, and had been in camp with the team this offseason before being released. Now, he’s back on the practice squad and could see an elevation coming soon. That marks the second addition at receiver this week, as the 49ers also signed former second-round pick Dante Pettis to the practice squad on Wednesday.

title: 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan weighs in on reviewable pass interference
summary: Nobdy signs up to watch “ref ball” on Sundays, but it seems like we can’t go a week in the NFL without the game being impacted by a controversial call. I’m sure the Arizona Cardinals felt like they were robbed on a couple of offensive pass interference calls against the San Francisco 49ers in Week […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nobdy signs up to watch “ref ball” on Sundays, but it seems like we can’t go a week in the NFL without the game being impacted by a controversial call. I’m sure the Arizona Cardinals felt like they were robbed on a couple of offensive pass interference calls against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 3. They were ticky-tack, but pale in comparison to what we watched on Sunday Night Football. Karma came for the Los Angeles Rams, who were on the wrong side of a pass interference call against the Denver Broncos. Rams cornerback Josh Wallace made an impressive play to intercept Bo Nix, but wide receiver Pat Bryant did his best NBA/World Cup impersonation, and flopped his way into a penalty on the defense, in what looked like an obvious offensive pass interference call after replay. NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay did not believe Rams CB Josh Wallace should have been flagged for pass interference, in what may have otherwise been an interception. The Broncos went on to score what would serve as the game-winning TD. pic.twitter.com/A0YDJ8ZmZl — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) September 28, 2026 Kyle Shanahan wasn’t asked about this specific play, but he was asked what he thought about the experiment with challenging defensive pass interference years ago, and if the NFL should bring it back: “I thought it was good going into it then because I’m always, regardless of what happens, I just want them to get it right. You just want it done right, and especially if you can see it on TV. It sucks to have to live with the wrong way when you’re in the heat of battle on the field, which is what the challenge is for refs, challenge for everybody. So, I was excited when they made pass interference challengeable back then. Then after going through that year, I don’t think I ever want it back because it got too much and there was too much let them play, too much slow it down and see a little. It almost probably would be like challenging fouls in the NBA. It just gets a little hard, so probably not a fan of it anymore.” The 49ers were fortunate that rule no longer exists, or else they would’ve been on the wrong side of the coin last week. Still, if it feels like the majority of calls go against the Niners, that’s because they have during Shanahan’s tenure: Every fanbase swears the refs screw them Here's every flag in crunch time since 2018 Are you getting robbed or getting bailed out? pic.twitter.com/5k0MMCH0YP — Stick to the Model (@StickToTheModel) October 1, 2026 Last week, Fred Warner was flagged by the back judge for an unnesscary roughness penalty that ultimately gave the Cardinals field position and gave them an opportunity to put points on the board. It felt like your run of the mill tackle that happens over the middle on every play. It wasn’t egregious, like Bryant’s against the Saints, but it helped keep the game close for Arizona. Some of the errors we’ve seen from the refs in recent weeks have been horrific. Hopefully, based on that chart above, the 49ers have better luck moving forward when it comes to the whistle. How did you feel about the rule? Would you like to the NFL bring it back? Let us know below in the comments.

title: 49ers expecting Mykel Williams to return as soon as he’s eligible after opening practice window
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have been ravaged by injuries at a couple of places, but none have been more impactful than their injuries on the defensive line. The 49ers lost six defensive linemen through the first two weeks of the season to injury, and they’ve had to make a number of roster moves to recover […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 2: Alfred Collins #95, Sam Okuayinonu #91, Jordan Elliott #92, Mykel Williams #98 and Keion White #56 of the San Francisco 49ers on the sideline during the game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on November 2, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The 49ers defeated the Giants 34-24. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have been ravaged by injuries at a couple of places, but none have been more impactful than their injuries on the defensive line. The 49ers lost six defensive linemen through the first two weeks of the season to injury, and they’ve had to make a number of roster moves to recover and stay afloat with enough bodies at the position. However, they did get one player back finally, as Mykel Williams saw his practice window open this week after starting the season on PUP. Williams is not allowed to return until Week 5, but gets 21 days to return after his practice window has opened. What is the plan for the second-year defensive lineman? “He looks excellent and it’s been a long time coming,” John Lynch said. “When you’re in those ACL, those long-term injuries, there’s a mental grind that comes with that, and I’ve been very proud of Mykel with how he’s handled it, how he’s embraced it. I know Mykel, he’s a coachable young man who’s going to say ‘yes, sir,’ but when we told him that, hey, we’re gonna put you on PUP and you’re not gonna be eligible until Week 5, I know he was upset, but he just went back to work. “I think now he’s in a good spot. We got to get from here to there, but it was nice to see him out there yesterday, and today we’ll get in some. He’s chomping at the bit to get out there. He’ll make us a better football team the second he’s out there and we’re looking forward to that time. He’s not eligible to play this week, so this week we can just open his practice window, and the following week he will be eligible provided things go well, we’re looking forward to seeing him out there.” It’s a good sign that Williams could be out there sooner rather than later because the 49ers could be facing some big tests soon. After the Denver Broncos this weekend, they’ll get the Seattle Seahawks in Week 5 on the road It is interesting that John Lynch expects Williams back when he is eligible, as his practice window was not opened last week, but he could slot in as an immediate starter and be a big help to their run defense, which has looked fine, but not great, through the first three weeks of the season. Currently, the 49ers are starting Keion White, Osa Odighizuwa, Gracen Halton, and Romello Height on the defensive line, with Khalid Kareem, Ogbo Okoronkwo, Naquon Jones, and James Thompson as depth. Williams had been coming on strong at the end of his rookie season, but that was cut short last year with his torn ACL. Still only 22 years old, the first-round pick has a ton of football ahead of him and will look to potentially hit the field in Week 5.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: John Lynch on Mike Evans: ‘Mike’s going to make every attempt to try to play’
summary: When the San Francisco 49ers lost Mike Evans during their Week 3 win over the Arizona Cardinals, the visible pain Evans was in looked like a player who would be out for longer than seven days. During a Thursday morning interview on KNBR, Lynch spoke about his star wide receiver’s toughness: “I will tell you […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the San Francisco 49ers lost Mike Evans during their Week 3 win over the Arizona Cardinals, the visible pain Evans was in looked like a player who would be out for longer than seven days. During a Thursday morning interview on KNBR , Lynch spoke about his star wide receiver’s toughness: “I will tell you this: Mike Evans, part of the whole package, when I talk to people like Ronde Barber, my old friend who’s stayed really close with the Bucs, once we got him, I think one of the things Ronde said first was, ‘That’s a tough SOB. And I think we’ve already seen that with Mike. You know, he is old school in his mindset, and he doesn’t want to miss.” Evans missed Wednesday’s session with the rib injury he sustained this past Sunday. Lynch isn’t ready to rule Evans out for Sunday just yet, though: “And so, we’ll always do what’s right for our player and all that stuff, but Mike’s going to make every attempt to try to play, and we’ll see where that goes. It’s still Thursday, and a couple more days before we kick off. He’s dealing with that, and we’ll see if he can get there by Sunday.” The 49ers could be down multiple receivers, as Evans wasn’t the only wideout to miss Wednesday’s practice. KhaDarel Hodge was a new addition with a knee injury, which explains Dante Pettis’s signing to the practice squad. Against the best secondary they’ve faced to date, the 49ers’ wide receivers could consist of: Deebo Samuel, Jacob Cowing, Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks, and Pettis this Sunday. Not yet for Nick Bosa The 49ers must’ve felt like Nick Bosa was closer to “week-to-week” since they didn’t place him on Injured Reserve. Bosa pulled his calf muscle in practice last week, missing Week 3. According to Lynch, it’ll be at least another week until we see the Niners’ best defensive player: “I think Nick’s doing well. He’s working diligently. I mean, it was just like a week ago today when that happened. And so, he’s worked really hard, and he’ll likely be out this week, and then we’ll go from there. And we’ll look forward to the time when we have Nick back.” Romello Height was limited on Wednesday. It’d be nice to get him back in the fold, especially if Keion White’s hamstring injury keeps him sidelined. The good news is White was working on the side of the field, so he may be able to contribute in Week 4. The 49ers aren’t going to rush Bosa back: “But when we bring him back, we’ve got to make sure he’s right on all counts, and he’ll work his tail off until he can get back out there. I think he’s working through it, and when he’s right, we’ll have him back out there. I’m not trying to be vague. Calf injuries are sometimes murky.” The goal without Bosa doesn’t change: Win more than you lose. A 3-0 cushion helps. Seattle falling in Week 3 did, too. But we know how unpredictable the NFL is, and the Niners could get upset just as easily. Weathering the storm until Bosa returns won’t be easy. Mykel Williams is likely a week away from returning, but it’s unfair to expect him to look like a first-rounder given the injury he’s coming back from.

title: Christian McCaffrey has chance to surpass Hall of Famer on Sunday
summary: Christian McCaffrey is regularly compared to Marshall Faulk because of his remarkable dual-threat ability as a running back. Before McCaffrey’s emergence, Faulk and 49ers legend Roger Craig were held up as the gold standard for backs who could do significant damage as a receiver as well as with their running ability. McCaffrey’s exceptional production on […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 27: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers runs with the ball during the first quarter of the game against the Arizona Cardinals at Levi's Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Christian McCaffrey is regularly compared to Marshall Faulk because of his remarkable dual-threat ability as a running back. Before McCaffrey’s emergence, Faulk and 49ers legend Roger Craig were held up as the gold standard for backs who could do significant damage as a receiver as well as with their running ability. McCaffrey’s exceptional production on the ground and as a pass-catcher for the 49ers has seen him join their ranks and establish himself as a clear all-time great dual-threat back. And, while his previous injuries may prevent McCaffrey from matching Faulk’s counting stats for his career, he can surpass the Hall of Famer on Sunday in one respect if he has a receiving touchdown on Sunday. Should McCaffrey haul in a touchdown reception against the Denver Broncos, that would mark his 37th receiving touchdown. That number would see McCaffrey move clear of Faulk (36) and claim the outright record for receiving touchdowns by a running back in the Super Bowl era. If McCaffrey has a touchdown of any sort and racks up at least 100 scrimmage yards, he will tie Jim Brown (55) for the fifth-most games with a minimum of 100 scrimmage yards and a score. Only Pro Football Hall of Famers Emmitt Smith (74), Faulk (66), LaDainian Tomlinson (61) and Barry Sanders (57) have more such games to their name. Faulk finished his illustrious career with 19,154 scrimmage yards, while McCaffrey has 13,249 after three games of his 10th NFL season. The math is against him bridging that gap, but it is highly likely he will snatch a piece of league history from Faulk in the very near future.

title: Kyle Shanahan downplays Broncos play caller change, calls talk ‘overrated’
summary: Off to a 3-0 start, the San Francisco 49ers are heading back home in Week 4, as they’ll face the Denver Broncos at Levi’s Stadium on Sunday in one of their early tests of the season. San Francisco’s offense has been humming early, despite a bevy of injuries, as Brock Purdy has played at an […]
full_text: DENVER , CO - SEPTEMBER 20: Offensive coordinator Davis Webb of the Denver Broncos reacts to a penalty called against his unit during the second quarter against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colorado on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images Off to a 3-0 start, the San Francisco 49ers are heading back home in Week 4, as they’ll face the Denver Broncos at Levi’s Stadium on Sunday in one of their early tests of the season. San Francisco’s offense has been humming early, despite a bevy of injuries, as Brock Purdy has played at an MVP-like level to start the season. The Broncos, on the other hand, haven’t looked as clean. They were a mess against the Kansas City Chiefs on both sides of the ball in Week 1. But they’ve had quality wins over the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams over the past two weeks, with the offense finally coming alive in Week 3. There was a lot of coaching talk regarding the Broncos this offseason, as head coach Sean Payton relegated playcalling to offensive coordinator Davis Webb in an effort to keep him in Denver. There have been some mixed results with the process, leading people to question whether that move was ultimately the right one. The 49ers have dabbled in the preseason with play-calling changes, as Kyle Shanahan has often passed the clipboard to Klay Kubiak, San Francsico’s offensive coordinator. What did he think of the change, and how could it affect Sunday’s game? “I’m sure it’s hard [on Davis Webb], but sometimes I think it’s overrated,” Shanahan said about the situation. “I guarantee, without me knowing, I guarantee Sean’s a big part of all of that on game day and during the week. It’s only been three games, so you can’t really tell yet. I mean, you can see over the course of the year, but sometimes I think that stuff’s made too big a deal about. “I can’t tell you how much Klay’s involved in what we do, and I call it so people give me the credit. But if he was calling it, it wouldn’t be much different either. It has to do with the plan that you do in the week. Most of the situational stuff you guys already have an idea where you’re going, and we all have a headset, so you can chime in on a lot of stuff anytime. So, I think a lot of that stuff’s a little overrated.” Of course, Shanahan has long been used to being the team’s play-caller in addition to head coach. How has he found the process beneficial over his coaching career? “Yeah, definitely. I enjoy it a lot, so that would kind of be hard, but it gets made such a big deal about just this day and age,” Shanahan said about play-calling. “My dad called plays for a long time, and then him and Gary [Kubiak] would switch it off all the time. Sometimes Gary would open the game and then he’d give it to my dad. Second quarter, they’d go back and forth. “When I was in Houston, Gary and I did that a lot. Sometimes I would take it, sometimes he would take it. It’d go back and forth. The main thing is who talks to the quarterback. It takes a little bit longer when the guy talking to the quarterback isn’t the guy calling plays, so that’s kind of the negative of it and that’s what is hard about going back and forth. But yeah, if I felt that was the best thing for our team, I’d for sure do it.” We’ll see how smooth that operation is for the Broncos in Week 5, as they’ll have to deal with a road environment once again. But Denver is experimenting with change early this season, and there have been some ups and downs so far.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 3 Titans who need to be way better vs. Ravens in Week 4
summary: The Tennessee Titans will play against Derrick Henry, Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4. The winless Titans need to be significantly better than they’ve been if they hope to execute an upset. We’ve identified three veteran players the team needs big-time performances from. QB Cam Ward It obviously starts with quarterback Cam […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans will play against Derrick Henry, Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4 . The winless Titans need to be significantly better than they’ve been if they hope to execute an upset. We’ve identified three veteran players the team needs big-time performances from. QB Cam Ward It obviously starts with quarterback Cam Ward. Believe it or not, the sophomore No. 1 overall pick did some good things versus the New York Giants in Week 2, including leading a possession where he completed 8-of-8 passing attempts and threw a touchdown. But Ward made two glaring red-zone errors that cost the Titans 14 points in a five-point defeat. The fanbase is beginning to sour on Ward. Sunday’s showdown with the Ravens will be his 21st career start. The Titans can’t admit defeat on a top-pick quarterback this quickly, but progress needs to start becoming evident. DE Jermaine Johnson II The offseason trade that sent T’Vondre Sweat to the New York Jets for defensive end Jermaine Johnson II is starting to age terribly. Sweat has made an instant impact in East Rutherford. Meanwhile Johnson doesn’t have his first sack with the Titans. All the advanced metrics (Pro Football Focus) say Johnson has been Tennessee’s least efficient pass rusher. Playing against Lamar Jackson and this Ravens offensive line is always a challenge. The Titans need way more from Johnson. CB Alontae Taylor PFF has Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor allowing 13 receptions on 15 targets for 116 yards. That’s a completion percentage of 86.7%. He also doesn’t have an interception or a pass breakup yet. Taylor has been serviceable on tape, but the Titans need more from their $19 million per year cornerback. Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers has been excellent through three weeks. Taylor will probably draw the coverage assignment on Flowers.

title: Derrick Henry says Titans didn’t try to re-sign him
summary: This is not surprising, but Derrick Henry said yesterday that the Tennessee Titans didn’t make an effort to re-sign him after the 2023 season: Look, there is an alternate universe where Mike Vrabel doesn’t get fired, and he pushes Ran Carthon/Amy Adams Strunk to try to bring Henry back. I’m not sure Henry even wanted […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - JANUARY 07: Derrick Henry #22 of the Tennessee Titans runs off the field after the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium on January 07, 2024 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is not surprising, but Derrick Henry said yesterday that the Tennessee Titans didn’t make an effort to re-sign him after the 2023 season: Derrick Henry confirmed the Titans didn't try to retain him before he joined the Ravens, via @jamisonhensley : "It was bittersweet … Good things don't last forever so it was time for me to find a new home." pic.twitter.com/AkhTXHutyk — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) September 30, 2026 Look, there is an alternate universe where Mike Vrabel doesn’t get fired, and he pushes Ran Carthon/Amy Adams Strunk to try to bring Henry back. I’m not sure Henry even wanted to re-sign here. He knew what the next couple of years were going to be like, and he wanted to go chase a ring. I don’t blame him for that. It has worked out really well for him. He’s been on a perennial playoff team and has solidified his case for the Hall of Fame. Henry even has an outside chance at breaking Emmitt Smith’s career rushing record. It’s been weird seeing Henry in a Ravens’ uniform. It will be even weirder watching him carry the ball against the Titans this week, but that’s how life goes for most NFL players. I love King Henry and will always be thankful for what he did for the Titans, but I hope he has 10 carries for 25 yards on Sunday.

summary: The 0-3 Tennessee Titans don’t have many bright spots following Week 3 and heading into Week 4. If there’s one encouraging thought, it’s that both first-round rookies played their best games versus the New York Giants. Wide receiver Carnell Tate and defensive end Keldric Faulk made standout impacts. Tate registered a team-high six receptions for […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Carnell Tate #14 of the Tennessee Titans runs a route during an NFL football game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 0-3 Tennessee Titans don’t have many bright spots following Week 3 and heading into Week 4 . If there’s one encouraging thought, it’s that both first-round rookies played their best games versus the New York Giants. Wide receiver Carnell Tate and defensive end Keldric Faulk made standout impacts. Tate registered a team-high six receptions for 58 receiving yards. Those were career-high marks for the fourth overall selection. Tate was peppered with nine targets, and is trending towards having his first double-digit target game soon. Cam Ward missed Tate in the end zone on a wide-open route on 3rd-and-goal. There were some other missed opportunities from Ward on tape, including on the game-losing interception . The former Ohio State standout was consistently creating separation and winning as a route runner. Faulk also registered his first career sack. The 31st overall selection ran a stunt with Jacob Martin. He looped outside and utilized his length to get the better of Giants Pro Bowl tackle Andrew Thomas. It was a nice glimpse into Faulk’s skill set, one the Titans thought was worth trading up for. Titans first-round pick Keldric Faulk picks up his first career sack! @TENvsNYG on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/HDvJapSKKH — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 Concerns had already been raised about both of Mike Borgonzi’s first-round selections. Tate has obviously been held back by one of the lowest-scoring offenses in the NFL. Sunday’s tape was a breakout game for Tate, even if the stats don’t yell breakout production. It was awesome to witness Faulk record his first career sack. The Titans need more pass-rushing production from defensive lineman other than Jeffery Simmons. If Faulk can continue showing progress, he should start playing more snaps, replacing Martin and Jermaine Johnson. Tate and Faulk are trending in the appropriate direction (even if the Titans are not). Let’s hope for follow-up strong performances from the first-round rookies versus the Ravens in Week 4.

full_text: The Commanders didn’t even wait for their formal injury report to announce the return of some key starters. Head coach Dan Quinn said that linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin) and tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring) will play on Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. That’s a huge win for Washington, getting two primary starters back in the lineup. Quinn also announced the quarterback Jayden Daniels was ruled out of Sunday contest after returning to practice on a limited basis while recovering from a dislocated left elbow. If you think we’re buried the lede here, we haven’t. Daniels got his own story, which you can read by clicking the link below: ⬇️ The team formally ruled safety Nick Cross (illness) and guard Sam Cosmi (concussion) out earlier in the week, as they weren’t part of Washington’s traveling party for this Week 4 contest against the Colts. Running back Rachaad White ’s only uncertainty heading into injury report’s formal release on Friday afternoon. He didn’t participate in practice all week due to a shoulder injury suffered in a Week 3 victory over Seattle. It seems likely he’s out, but Quinn didn’t say so directly during his Friday press conference. The Commanders brought newly re-signed running back Austin Ekeler with them to London and it’s possible he could suit up right away despite Washington running a different system than when he was with the team last season. This story will be updated after the Commanders and Colts release their injury reports. Check back for updated information.

But, as is typical of him, he was working very hard to get back, doing everything he can behind the scenes to do that as fast as he can. He is a true competitor on and off the field.” Mariota will start for a second straight game, fresh off an inspiring performance in a 33-31 victory over the Seattle Seahawks. full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Landover, Maryland, USA; Washington Commanders defensive tackle Tim Settle (97) celebrates with teammates after recovering a fumble against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Geoff Burke-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Commanders took the field in their home opener against the Seahawks, reeling from the Week 2 loss of their starting quarterback Jayden Daniels, adding to the injury attrition of key starters including LT Laremy Tunsil, RG Sam Cosmi, S Nick Cross, LB Frankie Luvu and TE Chig Okonkwo. The injury concerns were further compounded by the underperformance of secondary players Mike Sainristil, Quan Martin and Jeremy Reaves, combined with growing doubts about leadership of the head coach and new schemes on both sides of the ball being spearheaded by novice coordinators. Around the league, confidence in the Commanders was tanking following the devastating 20-37 Week 2 loss to the Cowboys. The Vegas line had the Commanders as 8.5-point underdogs at home, against the visiting Seahawks. What took place was a reminder of the generally mis-quoted, but nonetheless apt movie line about what can happen “on any given Sunday”. The rag-tag band of injury replacements, disrespected, and underrated players rallied around journeyman backup Marcus Mariota, who led an efficient offense that did enough to capitalize on opportunities generated by the defense, while avoiding turnovers. The defense was strong against the run (9 th fewest rushing yards allowed Week 3), but continued to struggle against the pass (32 nd in passing yards allowed). The key to victory was generating 3 turnovers which led to points, compared to the Seahawks’ 0. Historically, teams with a +3 turnover differential have a 90.7% win rate. That is a tremendous obstacle for an opponent to overcome. As good as Jaxon Smith-Njigba and the Seahawks’ passing attack may be, on Sunday it was not enough. In Week 3, missing their star QB and key starters on both sides of the ball, against the reigning Super Bowl champs, the Commanders’ offense ranked 20 th in the league in weighted EPA/Play at +0.04, while the defense ranked 11 th at -0.045: Image courtesy of RBSDM.com The upset win was the result of total team effort. Players making that kind of effort, in the face of the type of adversity the Commanders were facing, points to coaching and leadership perhaps being better than was widely appreciated. While the overall game left plenty of room for improvement, there were some standout performances on both sides of the ball, as well as continued struggles from players who have underperformed, and another key loss to injury. As the Commanders seek to carry the momentum with them to London, let’s take a look at who stepped up, who struggled and where everyone played in the biggest upset of the 2026 season so far. BIGGEST PLAYS OF THE GAME These plays had the biggest impact on a team’s scoring potential on a drive, as quantified by Expected Points Added (EPA). EPA -4.45 Q4, 4:09, 2 nd and 15 at WAS 49: Sam Darnold pass short middle intended for AJ Barner is intercepted by Kain Medrano at 50 and returned for 50 yards, touchdown. title: Washington Commanders vs Indianapolis Colts Week 4: Five Questions with Stampede Blue
summary: It’s week 4 of the NFL season, and the 1-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 1-2 Indianapolis Colts team at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET. The Colts are in a bit of a similar situation as the Commanders. The Colts also started the season 0-2, losing to the […]
full_text: It’s week 4 of the NFL season, and the 1-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 1-2 Indianapolis Colts team at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET. The Colts are in a bit of a similar situation as the Commanders. The Colts also started the season 0-2, losing to the Ravens in week 1 and the Chiefs in week 2, before winning an upset victory in week 3 against their division-rivals, the Houston Texans. The Colts coaching staff also find themselves on the hotseat and might consider this a must-win game despite how early it is in the season. On offense, the Colts are coached by HC Shane Steichen and OC Jim Bob Cooter, both of whom have been running the Colts offense since 2023. Washington fans may remember Steichen for his time as OC of the Philadelphia Eagles from 2021-2022. From his time with the Eagles and through to the Colts, Steichen has run a primarily shotgun-based offense ( 55.6% shotgun rate ) that makes heavy use of under-center formation and play action ( 20.3% play action rate, 3rd-highest in the NFL ). It’s hard to describe Steichen’s offense as it’s not exactly a West Coast offense and it doesn’t exactly fit into the mold of other offenses. Steichen’s offense is really a deceptively simple, yet flexible offense that attempts to create a lot of options from the same looks. It builds in lots of layers in the passing game, so that QBs have options to throw it to all levels of the field depending on what coverage is called. Its foundation is the run game, built around RB Jonathan Taylor, who combines track-star speed (running a 4.39 40-time) and elite tackle-breaking agility and power. The success of the run game sets up the play-action passing game, freezing pass rushers long enough to allow QB Daniel Jones to make deep throws all over the field. However, the Colts vertical passing game will be hindered with the loss of WR Alec Pierce to injury, as he was their primary field stretcher. Without Pierce, the Colts passing game has largely funneled through WR Josh Downs, who only received 4 targets in week 1 alongside a healthy Alec Pierce, but has received a shocking 20 targets over weeks 2 & 3 with Alec Pierce sidelined. Downs lines up primarily in the slot, so his potential matchup on CB Mike Sainristil will be something to monitor. On defense, the Colts are in their second season with DC Lou Anarumo, former longtime DC of the Bengals. Nominally, Anarumo runs a 4-3 defense, though in reality he makes heavy use of variable fronts and disguises. The Colts DL is headlined by former All-Pro DT DeForest Buckner and 2024 1st-round pick DE Laiatu Latu (who had 8.5 sacks last season). Anarumo had a DB coaching background before being elevated to coordinator, which shows in his variable coverage structures and heavy use of disguise and last-minute rotations in coverage. Anarumo’s defense ends up in man coverage at a 30.1% rate, 3rd-highest in the NFL . The problem with man coverage is it only works as well as its weakest link, so it requires multiple DBs who are good in man coverage. I think this is the reason the Colts signed former All-Pro CB Charvarius Ward in the 2025 offseason and traded two 1st-round picks for repeat All-Pro CB Ahmad “Sauce” Gardner during the 2025 season, probably believing that the latter would solidify the secondary. Unfortunately, that has not come to fruition, as teams continue to pick on the other weak links in the Colts secondary, primarily in the middle of the field. The result is a defense that has allowed the 3rd-most passing yards and 4th-most rushing yards through three games this year. A big part of the problem with this defense has been missed tackles . The Colts had 9 missed tackles against the Ravens in week 1 and 19 (!!) missed tackles against the Chiefs in week 2, before dropping down to 4 missed tackles against the Texans in week 3. It remains to be seen if the improvement in week 3 is a trend or a fluke. I asked Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue five questions to better understand the state of the Colts and what to look for in this game. 1) The Colts defense gave up more than 500 yards in each of their first two games, but managed to hold the Texans to 223 yards and 17 points. What did the Colts do more effectively on defense last week and do you think the defense will stay improved going forward or was last week more about the Texans struggles on offense? The Colts defense underwent some big changes this offseason jettisoning long time defensive leaders, Zaire Franklin and Kenny Moore. Fans were largely tired of Franklin’s on and off field antics and most believed Moore’s best days were behind him. Ultimately it was the right move to attempt a soft reset on a defensive leadership group that had yet to find any sort of sustained success. They remade the linebacker corps with a mix of rookies and mid to low tier free agent additions. They replaced Nick Cross with third round rookie AJ Halucy and overhauled the defensive line rotation. Ultimately, it’s going to take time for this defense to find their footing. Sunday was a good showing, no doubt. They did a great job stopping the run and rushing CJ Stroud, but I believe their success had more to do with Houston’s offensive ineptitude than it marking some sort of tide turning moment for the Indy defense. Each week we should see the defense make incremental improvements before finally getting up to speed around week 8 or 9. I will be skeptical until they perform well against a quality offensive opponent. 2) What is your opinion of Daniel Jones and is he the future of the franchise? By the way, when Jones was on the Giants, he always played his best games against Washington, so I’m not looking forward to this matchup. Daniel Jones is the guy Indy should have had starting at quarterback when they drafted Anthony Richardson. Jones is a fine quarterback when surrounded by a good supporting cast and good play caller/offensive system. You’ll win games with him, not because of him. Meanwhile, if the supporting cast or play calling break down, he can lose you games without strong defensive performances, when he presses too hard or tries to force plays. Last week was the perfect encapsulation of who Jones is. He largely kept the offense moving, made some really good throws, stayed on schedule, made good checks at the line and kept things running smoothly for the majority of the game. He also threw a baffling interception and gave up two fumbles on avoidable strip sacks. If not for those three plays, Jones would have been great against a very good Texans defense. Instead Indy was fighting for its life inside of a minute to play in the fourth quarter. 3) What is your opinion of GM Chris Ballard and HC Shane Steichen? Ballard has been in position since 2017 and Steichen since 2023, yet neither has seen the Colts win the division in their tenure. I have a lot of sympathy for Ballard. In his first year as GM he had Josh McDaniels back out as his first head coaching hire (in hindsight this was a good thing, but it was highly embarrassing at the time) despite having already started to fill out McDaniels’ coaching staff and having several of his handpicked coaches already under contract. He believed he was walking into a situation with a long-term answer at quarterback only to have Andrew Luck retire after his second season as GM. He has weathered every unprecedented storm that has come his way and stayed true to his vision and process. I really respect that. On the other hand, during his tenure the Colts have failed to develop into a winner. He used a 2023 top 5 pick on a (so far) busted quarterback and only got another year at the helm in 2026 because the first 8 games last season were a whole lot of fun to watch. title: What Commanders QB Jayden Daniels said about quick return from elbow injury
summary: Jayden Daniels has been practicing this week with a large brace on his left arm, something he’ll wear all season to avoid yet another elbow dislocation that he suffered last year and again in a Week 2 loss at Dallas.   His return to practice and eventually play has been faster than it was last […]
full_text: Jayden Daniels has been practicing this week with a large brace on his left arm , something he’ll wear all season to avoid yet another elbow dislocation that he suffered last year and again in a Week 2 loss at Dallas. His return to practice and eventually play has been faster than it was last time, after talking with medical professionals about the prospect of having surgery versus not. Daniels opted against (at least for now) having surgery during the season. His reasoning for it was simple. “I love football. I play football,” Daniels told on-site reporters in a Thursday press conference leading into Sunday’s game against the Colts in London. “I get paid to play football, so … With all my teammates, everybody’s hurting. For me, just being a leader and a guy to go out there and give it my (best) shot to go out there and play. I need to protect myself and stuff like that. I just love football. I have a passion for it.” Daniels said the possibility of having surgery after the season remains up in the air, with a decision on whether to do so being made that that time. There is at least a possibility that he could play on Sunday , with veteran backup Marcus Mariota as another option versus the Colts. The brace does not allow for a full range of motion, limiting the ability to fully extend his arm. Daniels said there was no discussion about wearing a brace as a precautionary measure and also said that there will be an “adjustment period” for getting used to playing with it, but that it does not impact how he throws or his throwing motion. He is not fearful of another dislocation , and seems primed to make a quick and productive return. “Everything I went through, everyone said I’d be good to go,” Daniels said. “But, right now, I’m just taking it day by day.”

full_text: (Photo by Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images) A month ago we announced the release of our new app, which you can find here or by searching SB Nation in your neighborhood app store. Quite a few of you have downloaded it over the past month and have been using it. The goal with this app was to make it easier to join the community, and specifically comment, read the comments, and make your own posts, as well as keeping all the community posts – articles on the front page, Feed posts from you – front and center. The results so far are encouraging. In fact, it’s helped us set a new all-time record for comments this month across all of SB Nation’s communities, and I want to thank you for that. One of the most exciting new features is the game chat. It makes it easier to follow along with the barrage of comments that come during games and gets to the heart of why so many of you spend time in our community. Faster loading comments and notifications when someone replies to your comments and Feed posts are creating a more fun experience that you’re not going to find anywhere else. We also wanted to elevate the community’s contributions by putting your Feed posts inside one stream alongside all the other articles from the site. To that end, more people have seen your posts and more people have commented on them. In fact, we’ve set single-day commenting records three different times since the season started. And if you prefer just reading our traditional front page articles, there’s an option at the top to do that. So, one month in, thanks for making us part of your routine. If you haven’t checked it out, you can get it for iOs or Android . And if you’re not an app user, that’s OK! We’re glad to have you following along in whatever way makes you most comfortable.

full_text: The Daily Slop – 1 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Washington Post (paywall) Jayden Daniels returns to Commanders practice with left arm brace View Link Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels practices Wednesday in Watford, England. (Alastair Grant/AP) Quinn said the Commanders will increase Daniels’s reps as the week goes on and decide his game status Friday. “We’re not going to put him out there before he’s ready,” Quinn said. “That’s why it’s important for us to trust the process.” If Daniels can’t go, Marcus Mariota will log his second straight start. He has completed 63.8 percent of his passes (19th in the NFL), averaged 6.3 yards per attempt (23rd) and thrown four touchdown passes over two appearances this season. He has avoided committing any turnovers and has helped the offense stay afloat — allowing Washington (1-2) to be patient with Daniels, even if the team’s record creates urgency. “He’s always a person that’s in good spirits, but you can tell that, this being the second time around, he’s comfortable with where he’s at,” Mariota said. “… He’s really just trusting everybody around him. Everybody’s best interest is for the organization and for him, and we’re going to do all that we can to help support him.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Run Defense Off To Strong Start One of the biggest turnarounds on the Commanders defense this year compared to last season has been the run defense. After three games, the Commanders are currently ranked third in the NFL with an average of 82 yards per game surrendered on the ground. Last year, they ranked third worst, with an average of 141.8 rushing yards per game given up. That’s a 60 yard per game swing from last year, and for reference of how big that is, if the Commanders 2026 average of 82 yards per game continued over 17 games, it would have been the top ranked run defense in the NFL in 2025. That’s a huge turnaround from last year, so how are the Commanders doing it? Well, the personnel certainly helps. General manager Adam Peters spent the offseason completely revamping the defensive front with new interior defensive lineman, new edge defenders and new linebackers. That definitely has played a big part of it, but another huge part of it is the scheme from new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. When Jones was hired, I wrote about how the Vikings defensive scheme that he’s brought to Washington had some key features . It starts on the back end. The Vikings, and now the Commanders, love to keep both safeties back deep prior to the snap. By keeping them deep, they can disguise their coverages and rotate either safety in either direction, or just play the core coverage concepts the team likes to use, which are quarters and Cover-2. In order to keep two safeties back deep, the defense has to make a sacrifice, which is playing light in the box. When teams are being overwhelmed in the box, the number one solution to help stop the run is put a safety down in the box to reinforce the numbers and give the defense a numbers advantage. But if this scheme wants to keep both safeties deeper, then the front has to make up for that. So one of the other key features of this defense is the 3-4 front. The Vikings play it a lot and the Commanders are using it now too. In a 3-4 front, you get three big interior defensive lineman on the field as opposed to just two in a 4-3 front. On top of that, you have two outside linebackers playing the edge, which gives you five defenders on the line of scrimmage. It becomes much more difficult for offenses to run the ball into those types of fronts because it’s harder to generate double teams, and even when you do get those double teams, you have multiple big defensive lineman capable of occupying both blockers and keeping the linebackers clean behind them. This has been one of the biggest keys to the Commanders success against the run so far this year. Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne were good against the run last year on the interior, but they played mostly in a 4-3 front and didn’t get enough support elsewhere. This year, Tim Settle has joined them as the nose tackle, and Shy Tuttle has rotated in behind Settle at times too. This gives them three big interior lineman that are capable of controlling the line of scrimmage. Let’s take a look at an example from the Seahawks game. The Commanders run defense has jumped from 3rd worst last year to 3rd best this year. What has been behind the drastic change? I broke it down: https://t.co/DaaaQMl0IA pic.twitter.com/zbMrjpNDk9 — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) October 1, 2026 The Athletic (paywall) Ranking the top-5 backup quarterbacks 2. Case Keenum, Chicago Bears: Lock may have the best stat line among the backup quarterback performances, but Keenum has the best storyline. It had been over 1,000 days since Keenum had started a game, thrown a touchdown pass or run for a touchdown. He checked off all of those boxes in primetime against an elite defensive coordinator and without much of a running game. Ben Johnson obviously deserves a lot of credit, but so does Keenum, who was particularly effective against the blitz. 1. Marcus Mariota, Washington Commanders: Since Mike Macdonald became their coach in 2024, the Seahawks have given up more than 30 points just three times: Week 5 last season against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, when Baker Mayfield was making an early MVP case; Week 16 last season in an instant overtime classic against 2025 MVP Matthew Stafford; and last week, against Mariota and the Commanders. The final line wasn’t as impressive as Keenum or Lock, but considering the circumstances of the opponent, a mediocre running game and a rookie play caller, Mariota has a strong case as one of the best backups in the NFL. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From ESPN: There’s a strong chance Mariota starts Sunday in place of Jayden Daniels, who was limited in practice Wednesday with a dislocated left elbow. If that happens, then Mariota will have performed a meaningful trifecta for himself: starting football games in three iconic soccer stadiums. The Commanders (1-2) play the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, home of the team of the same name. In those two games, Mariota lost to the Los Angeles Chargers on a failed two-point conversion at Wembley while playing for the Tennessee Titans; and to the Miami Dolphins in overtime last season.
